title: Excellent all-purpose GPSr
review_text:
I bought a Garmin 60CSx GPS receiver as a replacement for a Garmin eTrex Legend for the purpose of geocaching. My eTrex Legend has served me well (and continues to do so) but I wanted a GPSr with more functionality, better operation under heavy cover and expanded map coverage for hiking and road navigation. Researching GPSrs led me to this unit, and I have been very pleased with it. There are a couple of minor negatives that I have found, but these can probably be overlooked.

I am very pleased with the appearance of the screen when the unit is powered on. The display is bright and colorful, and easy to read in the light. This is true of the daytime display. The night display is not as pleasant, with a hard-to-see color scheme. Backlighting the night scheme makes it a lot easier to read but it is still less than ideal.

The unit's software is very intuitive, a menu- and icon-driven interface giving access to all of the features. I have found little need for the user manual since I fist started working with this device, as everything is clear and easy to find. Buttons on the unit make it easy to find the menus and to navigate without too much hassle.

The base map is nothing special but it is adequate for basic navigation. We have used it to follow our path down the interstate. It shows the major roads and also any waypoints that are close by.

The best feature of this unit, in my opinion, is its ability to navigate under heavy canopy. With my eTrex Legend there were times when my unit would simply not be able to get a lock. The 60CSx has yet to lose signal, even inside my living room. The accuracy does drop when there is sufficient cover but the important thing is that it doesn't drop completely.

One thing troubles me a bit about the 60CSx. The accuracy rarely gets any better than 10-12 feet, whereas my eTrex Legend - a unit costing a third as much - routinely can get down to 6 feet. I do not understand why this is the case. I would choose ability to hold a signal over pinpoint accuracy every time, but why can't I have both?

The 60CSx has a Micro-SD card inside and the unit will take a card up to 2GB inside. That's enough room for a whole US street map. This is a nice thing to have available, as it means not having to decide what section of map to load. Load the whole map and be on your way.

The waypoint management functions are acceptable for my needs, which up to this point has meant managing geocaching waypoints. I like being able to mark a point as "found" and then being asked if I want to go to the next closest point. I have noticed, though, that if I am navigating to a point and leave the navigation menus, the point is marked as found anyway. It would be nice to have the ability to specify "not found" without having to go through the menus to locate the point again, just to change the status.

The Garmin 60CSx is a very nice handheld GPS that will serve you well. It is not perfect, but for general use it is plenty close enough.

title: Nice Entry-Level Unit
review_text:
I was given one of these units as a gift and I have been working with it for a couple of years now. I upgraded to a more capable and more expensive unit but I still use the eTrex Legend frequently. It is a fine entry-level GPS receiver (GPSr) for most applications.

First off, this is not a large and bulky unit but rather it fits nicely in the hand (or in a front pocket if desired). It is lightweight and the curves/shape do not make it uncomfortable to use.

In spite of being fairly small, the display is large enough to read clearly and the controls are fairly easy to use. There are a few buttons on the side of the unit as well as the "click stick" that facilitate navigating the menus and displays, but it is a good idea to read through the manual to get some idea of how these work. I took the unit out of the box and had no idea what to do or how to use it, but once I leafed through the manual it made good sense.

It takes some time to acquire the satellite fixes it needs to facilitate navigation. On average, it takes about 45 seconds to acquire a lock, which may or may not be acceptable to some people. For my purposes it is fine. That said, it does not take a lot to lose the fix - heavy canopy cover or even obstructing the reception by holding the unit with one's hand over the internal antenna can cause it to lose track, after which it cuts off to conserve battery power. So, this unit performs best under open sky or light cover, though I have had success even in very heavy cover.

The accuracy on this unit is quite good. I have seen it accurate to within 6 feet, which is excellent. It usually holds its accuracy fairly well, though sometimes it struggles when there is magnetic disturbance or heavy cover. It have difficulty in the car unless it is on the dashboard or near a window.

I use this unit almost exclusively for geocaching, and it has proven to be excellent for that purpose most of the time. It can hold up to 1,000 points and it has functions for managing waypoints. That said, my family and I connected it to the computer on a trip one time and used it to navigate from Virginia to Indiana, and it did a nice job of keeping up with the roads. Also, the batteries lasted from Washington DC to Indianapolis, under continuous use, about 12 hours.

The base map within is fine for *general* navigation but it is not very helpful for pinpointing. It will get you down the interstate and to major roads, but that's about it. Still, for a unit in its price range, that's reasonable. There's 8 MB of memory in the unit so more detailed maps can be loaded.

This unit has been dropped, stepped on, knocked off desks, sat on and otherwise abused, and it continues to work.

There are more powerful GPSrs that have more functionality, have a better display or have better reception in areas where this unit fails. Those units cost more. This is an entry level unit and it does quite well in that role.

It is certainly not perfect, but even at full price it is a good deal for what you get. It is NOT a top-of-the-line gaming rig but it's not marketed as such. title: Double protection feature. Strong construction.
review_text:
This is the perfect size for an ASUS Zenbook, with dongles attached. There are so many Neoprene sleeves to choose from on Amazon, I am very happy I chose this one.

1. Double zipper on top. This is a very sturdy zipper with zipper-pulls that are large enough to grab very easily. The zipper seams are sewn in evenly from edge to edge and zipper action is really smooth.

3. In addition to the padded protection of the Neoprene, the main compartment is lined with a baby-soft small pile shearling-type material, which also protects your mobile device from scratching. I love this added feature.
4. The handles are a feature that I was looking for. These handles are stiff and have a strong Velcro closure at the top. The handle is strong and well attached. No fear of them tearing. Personally, I would have preferred more of a canvas/cloth like handle which would be easier to grip. This handle is stiff and a little uncomfortable to grasp ( Handles are a bit big in my hand, so I find I am periodically adjusting my grip as I am walking) However, this is a minor inconvenience compared to the overall quality.
5. The Amazon price is fantastic! The quality is excellent for the price.

I highly recommend this product

review_text:
WOW! I've had this for about a month now and it is really great! Use this when I work from home or I am on the road. Blazing fast. Light as a feather. Easily connected to Bluetooth keyboard and mouse. The dongles work perfectly. At home I have extended the desktop to the ASUS IPS monitor - no problem. Sound is really good. I have not had any problem with the location of the power button or keyboard layout that other reviewers experienced. This is a great work-box for me. My 'work' computer was my HP Envy, which is a great laptop.......I find myself using the Zenbook more and more when working at home. This has also replaced my Samsung Galaxy Tab 10 as my 'mobile' tablet. So light and thin; easy to take with.

PROS
Super, super fast - this is the most responsive laptop I have ever owned
Incredibly light and thin - so portable, you will take it with you all the time.
super responsive keyboard & touchpad
touchpad auto-disconnects when Bluetooth mouse is enabled(sweeeeeeeet)
Easy to extend desktop with a VGA dongle
Connected Bluetooth devices perform perfectly - no drag at all
WIN10 is pre-installed

CONS
The power supply is a large, square 'plug' that covers at least 2 of the outlets on your surgestrip. Terrible design :-(
Dont buy if primary use will be Video streaming - glass screen is like a mirror/glare is a problem with video - difficult to find a video glare-free angle
There is a known WIN10 issue where pop-up dialog boxes are super-small and are extremely difficult to use. Microsoft is working on it
The first thing you should do is uninstall Macafee (pre-installed) - blocks so many apps., including Chrome (sigh)

UPDATE 03/29/2017
Just an FYI - I use this daily and love it, however I am now noticing the battery is getting hot after an hour or so of use. This is a new development. I am not sure what is causing this, but did want to share. I think I may have to shell out some cash for a new battery, which would be unfortunate. I have never had a laptop battery heat up like this before and have never had to replace a laptop battery. Not sure if others are having the same issue, over time.

title: Lovely little smartwatch, would make a great gift
review_text:
There are a lot of things I like about this smartwatch. The face is smaller than other smartwatches I've looked at and tried, about 1.09" which is perfect for me. Bigger faces like many smartwatches out there are uncomfortable for me to wear, especially when I'm trying to sleep. The design of the watch is really pretty, and I like how the neutral color goes with many outfits. One thing I do wish is that the watchband was changeable so that I could change it if the band wore out or broke (or if I wanted a different style). Most of the smartwatches with changeable bands are those with the large face, a little disappointing. Battery power is good. I use the smartwatch quite often so I tend to hook it up to the battery charger twice a week. I like how I could choose from a variety of screen displays to fit what my preferences are.

The app this smartwatch uses is great, the Da Fit app. It's super easy to use, you don't have to use Bluetooth to find the watch, you just use the app to find it. I like how it has a variety of physical activity you can choose to monitor, jogging, biking, walking, etc. The sleep feature is pretty good, the biggest detractor is that it only follows typical sleeping hours. It won't work for anyone who sleeps different hours due to working night shift. Hopefully they'll update that in the app someday. The blood pressure feature seems to be pretty accurate to what the doctor tells me my blood pressure is.

Since I really don't want to put out the money for the brand name smartwatches, I am very pleased that I can still enjoy quite a few of the features for a more reasonable price. I'd recommend this watch and it would make a great gift.

Update- After a couple weeks of use, the on/off button on the side of the watch popped off and a spring came out. It's so tiny I'm unable to find it. I wasn't using it excessively, so I'm disappointed that something on the watch would break within weeks of use. It's a really nice watch, and they have great customer care so hopefully my issue is not a common problem.

title: Still going strong after four years
review_text:
My husband bought me this camera as a surprise Christmas present about four years ago and it quickly became my favorite camera. It has been my camera of choice for two trips to Disneyland, a trip to Disney World and a cruise. It's a fantastic camera, and very easy for someone not technologically skilled like me to understand how to use. Battery life is great, I'm able to go through about two days of consistent use on our trips before I need to recharge. Speaking of which, recharging is a cinch, I bring the little charger, plug it in at the hotel room in the evening and by the next morning I'm ready to go (usually takes less than that but I plug it in and go to bed).

My only problems have been with trying to use the camera in lower lighting situations, like at my children's school assemblies and performances. Perhaps I'm not using the settings correctly but those pictures are coming out too dark with the colors off.

This has been one of the best presents ever. We're headed for another trip next year and this camera will be on my "must pack" list.

title: Worked ok for 1 1/2 years, then died
review_text:
We bought this Netgear WGR614 router back in March 2006. It installed somewhat easily and except for a little problem with the wireless PC card for the laptop (wouldn't be recognized at first but easily corrected) we had pretty stable use for about a year. Then we began to have connection problems. The connection would get slower and slower until internet pages would just not load, resulting in repeated "page cannot be displayed" errors. Powering down and restarting the router, modem and computer seemed to correct the issue. But as of this morning the router appears to have completely died. Powering down and restarting does nothing, the internet connection cannot be re-established. We can connect the desktop directly to the cable modem but for now the laptop is without connection, making for some unhappy family members here.

As of right now I don't know if we'll be buying another Netgear router & wireless PC card. The life expectancy of Netgear products does not appear to be all that great. Looking at some of the reviews we appear to be quite lucky that we got as much time out of the router as we did. Still I'm not in the mood to be shopping for a new router every 1.5 years or less. Hopefully there is a good router out there that can last at least two years.

review_text:
After doing some research, I read that these headphones are the best "bang for your buck" earbuds and so far, they aren't wrong. This product does some with six different silicon eartips, an small instruction booklet, and a small but durable pouch to put your eartips and buds in. It took me about five minutes find the perfect removable eartips for my ears. It would have been shorter but I was afraid of tearing the silicon tips (so far none have ripped). Everybody's ears are different but my ears prefer the smallest snowman shape ones for both my right and left ear (Pictures of the tips can be found in the 'Wired' only version of this product).

They are easy to clean and the remote is secure (meaning that the remote button or volume slider won't move or activate if it accidentally hits your clothes or something). I haven't used the microphone yet. These things are very secure once you install them in your ears. You can talk, yawn, chew gum, run, jump and drink water and these tips wouldn't budge (you can take them out easily though). The sound quality and noise blocking are great too for when I run. It also works well for people that wear glasses like me.

However I have two small issues with this product. One is that the wire is a little long for me but it usually doesn't get in your way (only once so far but this was my second time using them). You may experience burning in your ears. I did at first when I was trying to find the best way to wear them. For me (using the smallest snowman ones), You just put them before the ear canal so the silicon tips rest comfortably in your ears. Don't push/force them in your ears because that will cause your ears to burn.

In conclusion, if you're looking for the best sleek 'bang for your buck' earbuds that stay secure during rigorous activity who doesn't mind a little burning in your ear canals at first, then I would recommend this product and I'll probably buy it again when/if this product wears out.

Edit: Just after a month of use the the remote button is a little glitchy. Before it could be resting against by chest while running and it would work fine. Now while running, I have to pull it about 5 inches away from my body and point the the top of the headset (where it branches off into two) at about a 45 degree angle in order to pause/skip a song. It's kind of cumbersome and if it didn't do this then I'd definitely rate it higher.

Edit: The sellers were very prompt and understanding with my situation and I got a new pair for free (under warranty). I've been using them for a couple of months and I haven't noticed any problems with them.

title: Great Product! But even better customer service!
review_text:
I bought this EVGA CLC 280/280mm AIO a few months ago but I wanted to try it out for a while before I left a review to really get a chance to see how it performs over a longer period of time.

Firstly, I am running this AIO on an i7 8700K WITH an overclock of 5GHz on all cores. With this AIO my idle temperatures are in the mid to high 20C range and under full load it warms up to the low to mid 80s C. This is great performance for such a high overclock. With stock clock speeds this AIO should perform much better and shouldn’t go above 65C during full loads.

Secondly, I want to share my experience with EVGA’s superb customer service. When I installed this AIO I had a problem with the RGB not working. I tried reinstalling it, using different motherboard plugins for the cables, but nothing seemed to fix it. Finally I contacted EVGA by email. They mentioned that the USB cable could be defective. Here is what amazes me: EVGA sent me a brand new USB cable at no cost to myself and they didn’t even make me go through the hoops and hassle of sending my product back, paying for shipping, waiting for processing, etc., they just sent me a brand new cable and THEY paid to have it shipped. I got it 2 days later.

That is the kind of customer service I love and is the reason I try to buy EVGA products when possible. Most companies will not do that. They’ll put you through the hassle of many steps and lots of waiting around and processing which discourages a lot of customers, such as myself, from even bothering to contact them when something goes wrong.

All in all, a great product with even better customer service!

Thank you EVGA!

title: Great SSD for SMALL workloads.
review_text:
I’ve had this SSD for a few days and I also have a 1TB 970 Evo Plus and 1TB 860 Evo and all of them are great! But they do have their drawbacks too.

This drive does really well with SMALL (under 15Gb) workloads. The speeds are right up there (~500MB/s R/W) with my 860 Evo until it gets to about ~14GB at which point it slows down drastically. This is fine for things like boot, games, apps, and most programs.

However, if you do heavy workloads like video editing, file transfers, etc,. where you are regularly moving large (15GB+) files around this is NOT the drive for you. If you are a “heavy” user I highly recommend the 860 Pro. It can keep up those high R/W speeds without slowing down after ~15GB. It will maintain full speed throughout the duration of whatever you are doing.

With that said this is a great drive for light/moderate workloads (gaming, web browsing, small work files, etc.,) and it is at a price that gives you excellent value and quality for your money.

I also really love the Samsung Magician software. It’s basically the main reason why 3/5 of my drives are Samsung. Samsung is also known for making reliable, high quality products. Yes there is a premium compared to cheaper drives but you’re paying that little bit extra for quality & reliability.

I took off 1 Star on this review though because Samsung doesn’t include any of the cables or mounting screws which just doesn’t make sense to me. C’mon Samsung start adding that stuff! I would’ve happily paid a couple dollars more for it and it wouldn’t have cost Samsung that much so they could’ve made a little bit of extra profit by adding it.

I still recommend this drive though and would buy it or the 860 Evo again if I needed more storage.

title: Great SSD for the price
review_text:
Update: I see a lot of people complaining about the drive capacity being “wrong” (465gb instead of 500gb or 960gb instead of 1TB) and to those people I highly recommend going to YouTube and searching “What is Overprovisioning?” and clicking on the link by TechQuickie.

Samsung is NOT falsely advertising. The drive DOES in fact come with the advertised space it’s just that in order for it to work properly and perform optimally it requires approximately 10% of the capacity to be overprovisioned free space.

This is a really great SATA SSD for the price. It's perfect for storing games that have long load times without paying a fortune for an NVMe SSD of equal capacity. title: Everything fits, great price, not bad!
review_text:
UPDATE (4 -> 5 stars)/ 9/20/2013 - This thing is $28 now! You'd be nuts NOT to get this case! I'm pretty sure they're taking a loss selling it at that price, maybe they're overstocked and trying to get rid of them? If you're going to buy this case BUY IT NOW!

Firstly, I just want to say if you want to SEE my PC check out the last 3 customer uploaded images, they are of my newly built PC in this case. If you can't find customer images, go to the main product page for this case, and click "See all 5 customer images", it's right under the picture of the case.

My current specs:
CPU: AMD FX 8320 (3.5GHZ stock) Overclocked @ 4.22 GHZ
CPU Cooling: Corsair H80 High Performance Liquid Cooling System
Motherboard: Gigabyte FX 990 UD3 AM3+
Power Supply: Rosewill Capstone 750W 80+ Gold certified.
SSD: Sandisk 32GB (I just use it for my operating system for quick bootups, nothing else.)
HD: Seagate Barracuda 1TB 64MB cache 7200 RPM SATA III
Graphics: Geforce 760 GTX 4GB 256bit GDDR5 (When I was deciding whether or not to order this case, this was my biggest concern, "Will one of the new big geforce graphics cards fit?" - YES it will! I MIGHT be able to fit another one in, but I really don't need another one, the 760 is a beast!)
Ram: 16GB Gskill Sniper Series DDR3 2400

Whew, now having said all that, EVERYTHING fits in this case. Is it a little bit snug? See for yourself, I don't think so, but some might. I also got a non-modular power supply so that adds alot of unnecessary cables.

The fact is though, my computer does NOT overheat. I monitor temps whenever my computer is on (with CPUID, free program!) and as an example, under a full load my CPU temp stays ~20C and my GPU can get up to ~60C on a warm day. Keep in mind though for the CPU I'm using a $104 liquid cooling system (I just happened to get a GREAT deal on it).

The see-through case is pretty cool too, I like being able to see the components plus with a liquid cooling system if any liquid starts leaking I can immediately take care of it, although I highly doubt it will leak.

Anyway, I hope this review helps, keep in mind I put alot of stuff in here with the 4 ram modules, and the pretty large graphics card (the Geforce 760 GTX is about 11.5" long, it's pretty big), but it does all fit!

Keep in mind this is a ~$50 case. For $50 it is a good deal, if you want a "better" case, you're going to have to spend more money it's as simple as that. People nitpick things like a flimsy backplate, or not having the best cable management, well the more you expect from a product the more you're going to end up paying for it. So take it easy on a $50 case.

I can say for sure it's better than my old HP desktop PC computer case. It actually FEELS like a gamer's case.

So all-in-all, if you're on a budget and looking for a nice computer case for $50 I recommend this case. It's got everything I needed and it's got everything 90% of people will need or care about. I'd buy it again.

title: Working Thus Far
review_text:
My modem was 6 years old and wasn't working properly anymore. I did not want to pay the $150 for a new modem that Centurylink was offering. I found this product and decided to take a chance with it.

Set up was surprisingly not too much of a headache. I plugged in the power cable, the phone line cable, and then I plugged an Ethernet cable in from the modem in to my laptop. These three cables were included with the product. I did call the Centurylink technical support. She asked for the serial number on the modem to connect the modem to their network. After that, it was very simple, I entered in to the browser "connect.centurylink.com" and it gave step by step instructions. Once internet was connected, I set up a new SSID and WiFi password by entering in the modems IP address: 192.168.0.1. Everything is up and working as it should. I will update this review if I have problems in the future. I would like this modem to last at least a couple years.

The seller included a page of set up instructions/hints and it was complete garbage. It was broken English and misspelled words. It wasn't helpful in the slightest. Don't bother using it. Information was incorrect even. The IP address given is for an older model modem.

title: Without question this is one of my new favorite things
review_text:
These earbuds combine incredible sound in a stylish and functional package. I would give these more than 5 stars if I could. I had high expectations before trying these, especially in view of the price, and these earbuds blew those away.

Bang & Olufsen's engineers magically crammed a high-end sound system into a lightweight, wireless earbud. You have to hear them to believe how amazing these sound - clean, clear music across an impressively wide range. I noticed details for the first time in songs that I have heard many times before.

Beyond the sound, the craftsmanship and overall product design are outstanding. I don't know about the electronics as only time will tell, but the earbuds and the case themselves look like they will hold up to regular use without any issues. The leather and brushed aluminum on the case adds an extra-premium feel to the product.

Also, at first I thought the charging capability of the case was a bit gimmicky, but I quickly realized my error. It is so convenient to know that the earbuds are fully charged whenever I want to use them. I don't have a Qi charger, so I haven't taken advantage of the full wireless capability. But for me, it is not a big deal to use the USB cord when I need to occasionally charge the case.

To give some context, this is not a product I would have considered purchasing on my own. I've always thought of earbuds as cheap, portable ways to listen to music while working out or on the go - situations where the background noise means that you can't appreciate high-quality sound. However, after jumping at the chance to try these, they have completely changed my perspective on what earbuds can do. Excellent sound quality is available in a highly portable, convenient product.

The only downside I have experienced is that the touch controls take some time to get used to. I had trouble figuring it out at first, but after a few days I can usually get them to do what I intend to do on the first try. I prefer the minimalistic design, so this learning curve is not a significant issue for me.

I also like the Bang & Olufsen music app that allows selection of different listening modes that vary between - "warm", "excited", "relaxed", or "bright" sound profiles. Switching between the modes really gives the sound a different character. My favorite feature on the app, however, is the ability to select "transparency" of the music. A higher level of transparency amplifies your surroundings so you can hear what is going on around you. This does not give you spy-gadget levels of hearing, but it noticeably amplifies background sounds. I've been using these headphones at work, and I can easily hear when my phone rings or when someone knocks on my office door.

Last, the excellent sound quality carries over to phone calls. I have no trouble hearing the other person on the line, which is not always the case with the built-in speaker on my iPhone. Also the people I have talked to have had heard me clearly. This was an unexpected bonus, and I actually prefer to use the earbuds for calls now.

TL;DR: If you can afford these, you won't regret it.

On that note, be sure to check with SiriusXM.com for specific subscription costs before you buy a radio to help you choose whether you want a Sirius or XM radio.

I learned this the hard way. I hope this saves you some time and hassle.

title: Very thorough, lightweight software
review_text:
I have been running Internet Security for several months and have been very happy. I am sticking with this program in lieu of the more expensive and boggy "Total Protection" ... a so called upgraded version.

I prefer this basic lightweight version of McAfee Anti Virus/Malware protection, it doesn't bog down your system. The cache cleaner (QuickCleaner) is also very handy.

** Better yet/Best deal: buy the 2010 or 2011 subscription version and McAfee automatically downloads the 2013 updated files for 1 year.
[[ASIN:B003VUNYIG McAfee Internet Security 2011 - for up to 3-Users]]
McAfee Internet Security 2010 or 2011 - for 1 or up to 3-Users (currently selling for $1 - $7) Screaming deal!

Your subscription is good for 1 year from the time that you install.

Never renew through McAfee, too pricey. Just buy another old version and update the license code.

I tried the McAfee Total Protection version and hated it. Super Boggy software. After 1 week the software broke and would not update, created registry errors, and hosed up my pc. The File Lock "feature" kicked in with every attempt to update and I had to reboot to reconnect to the internet every hour or two while troubleshooting the problems myself. Pain in the behind. Don't do it!

Forget about "Technical Support" from McAfee. They claim 24/7 support, which will get you their super slow Chat "support". The Call Center doesn't work 24/7. Go figure. Both Chat and/or thier phone/remote assistance is a joke, plan on spending up to an hour while you wait for the connection, then wait longer while they muddle their way through an attempt at troubleshooting. Either way, you will eventually be connected to an unnamed Eastern country, and waste a whole lot of time and patience dealing with those numb nuts. I swear during the 3 contacts that I made to them, they must have been texting their buddies while I waited for responses which came at a snails pace (over 5 minutes for each response, no kidding!). I ended up uninstalling myself after 1 hour on my 3rd tech support call they wanted to uninstall it for me and reload. No I don't think so. I permanently uninstalled and went back to Intenet Security.

Travel light and go with the basic Internet Security version for AV & malware protection. It has all of the basics: firewall, AV scanner (email, realtime & scheduled scans), online backup addon, network protection, cache cleaner, email anti spam, and parental controls. That is all that I have needed, and have been happy with it. Hopefully I won't ever have to deal with their under qualified tech staff again.

Other options: Kaspersky is great software, but boggy and too many options to set up. I also used AVG in the past, but it didn't offer the best protection and I had undetected invasions. ESET has the best reputation, but I have never used it.

Steer clear of Norton for AV/Malware: generates a migraine magnitude headache. Nothing but problems. However, their Ghost program is good.

I hope that this review saves you some money, time, and frustration.

title: Not bad.
review_text:
Was actually pleased by the caps when they arrived. I used to be particular about keycap quality, but in the last few years the quality and cost of keycaps have been awesome; I'm so thrilled about those new to the hobby (although it's still expensive). When GMK 9009 was originally announced, I thought it was the perfect modern edition of classic beige. Everyone should have a good classic beige set, and 9009 is it.

Right now, my workhorse keyboard is a polycarbonate 910 with Cherry MX Grays and third-party springs (I forget the weight). Typing on it is a dream every day, and the keycaps can enhance the experience. I prefer PBT on this keyboard because it has a more pleasant, thocky sound than ABS caps. There's also a bit of tactile pushback with ABS, at least from what I noticed. While I love 9009, I'm not thrilled about ABS. Sure, ABS is cool and develops a nice shine based on use, but I prefer the consistent feel of PBT; having some keycaps stripped of their coating from use while others still feel new can throw me off. All that to say that I'm glad I was able to get this 9009 set in PBT. I was very hesitant, though, because the price for this many dye-sublimated, PBT keycaps was too good to be true.

When the package arrived, I was disappointed to find that there was no shipping box. The keycaps arrived in their manufacturer box with a shipping label slapped on it. Not only can that increase the chances of theft, but the shipping label covers the rendering that shows all the keycaps included. So now I'll have to resort to the listing to see what all should be in the box. However, nothing appears damaged. The keycaps come in wonderfully secure, plastic trays, three stacked on each other. There are a lot of keycaps here, so most keyboards should be covered. Of course, not everything will be perfect; for my 910, the Home cap is taller than the rest of the row, and there is no 1u Tab cap, nor a R1-height Fn cap. There's only one 1u blank keycap, which doesn't sit flush with the rest of the caps in its row. Minor gripes because I know my layout is particular.

But, again, there still is a great amount of keycaps so I'm sure most boards will be covered.

Now, as for the keycaps themselves. As I mentioned, I was very hesitant when the package arrived, but overall I'm pleasantly surprised. The keycaps are slightly thinner than enjoyPBT and BSP caps, and the stem can be a bit snug, but not too tight so that they don't come off easily. The sublimation is very good; I haven't noticed any that appear sloppy. Some num pad legends seem a bit thinner than others, but overall the legends are consistent and have that Cherry-legend appearance.

I wish there were more color options here, but for the price I can't complain. Truly, at $40, this set is an amazing bang for the buck.

title: Robust.
review_text:
This monitor has been versatile for my needs. I've used it as a second display for both a MacBook Pro and a Windows machine, as well as a monitor for my MiSTer FPGA setup. No matter what device you use, though, the monitor itself doesn't have digital settings. There are volume buttons, a power button, and ports for HDMI and type-C HDMI, but that's it. Everything else is controlled by the device it's plugged to.

For both computers I used, the computer picked up the monitor immediately. Because the monitor isn't UHD, the difference between the displays is striking, but I figured as much. I wish there was a way to fine-tune the monitor with its own settings. Some text can be a bit fuzzy and images a little pixelated. They're not too much of a noticeable difference, but still noticeable.

With my MiSTer gaming setup, the monitor was great too. With retro gaming, input latency is important. I noticed no added latency. I love that I can now move my gaming setup to wherever I please. The speakers are pretty darn good, too.

The stand could use refinement. It doesn't stay up easily and requires a few attempts before it stays up.

title: Wrong instructions and wobbly, but still fun to use.
review_text:
Before ordering this telescope, I researched the difference between reflector and refractor telescopes. The last telescope I had was a hand-me-down (I forget which brand) refractor telescopes. I've developed a strong passion for everything beyond earth, so I looked forward to using this telescope--my first reflector telescope.

Because the telescope requires assembly, I pulled out the instructions...and became very confused. While some of the parts looked similar to what was in the box, I quickly realized the instructions were for a completely different model. Even if these were the right instructions, the photographs provided were taken by a camera and not the clearest quality; good assembly instructions usually have computer-generated images or diagrams, not photographs taken by a camera. The rest of the instruction manual was a general guide on using telescopes, though a much better quick-start guide can be found easily online.

So, with some trial and error, and a lot more time than I anticipated building the telescope, I finally got it assembled. And just in time too, because the moon had just crossed the window of the room I build the telescope in, and the moon was in great view. The opportunity also let me play around with the features of the telescope. It's not very easy to use because the stand is *very* wobbly. The counterweights are too much for the tripod, and the tripod should have used a better, more sturdy material. The dials and weights are easy to use, but the tripod makes everything longer to set up because the view won't always stay while moving.

Despite all that, it's super fun to use. It comes with decent eyepieces to play around with; I didn't know how much of a difference eyepieces can make. With this telescope, I was able to view details of the moon for the first time. It really is just a big ball of rock spinning around.

title: Mostly excellent, but does disconnect once in a while.
review_text:
Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on.

Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4.

The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying.

Now for the good.

The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look.

This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

title: Fantastic system; so-so firmware.
review_text:
This is the first mesh system I've used. I had a Linksys router and an Asus router before this, both installed with third-party firmware. After the Asus upgrade, I used the Linksys router as a repeater. The signal was okay; considering I had Xfinity 250Mbps, the Asus worked fantastically, while the Linksys trailed behind. We live in an old apartment building with thick, plaster walls, so signal can be very spotty.

With this mesh system, I saw a huge upgrade the first week. Setup was very easy; quick instructions are provided. As soon as the setup was complete, I delved into the firmware. I recall being a little disappointed as I was used to the Asus custom firmware (Asuswrt-Merlin). The Asus firmware "just werqed." I run a small server, and setup was super easy with the Asus. With the Netgear, it was a lot more involved. Setting up outside ports was a pain; at the time, there was no simple way of forwarding ports. I recall a little workaround I was able to conduct with the server, but it took me days to figure out.

The firmware also lacks time restrictions for devices (at least of this writing). Asuswrt-Merlin allows me to set specific times to shut off internet for devices, which comes in handy with a large family.

As for the actual mesh system, so far so good. I can't tell when I'm using the main router or the satellite. The devices connect automatically without hiccup. I've since ditched Xfinity in favor of RCN 1Gbps; this mesh system works very well with the service. Once we have fiber, I can't wait to see the results.

title: Serious upgrade from Master 2.
review_text:
Even after using both MX Master 2 and 3, my favorite mouse still is the Proteus Core G502. Does that mean I don't like the Master 2 or 3? Yes and no. Yes to 2, no to 3.

I prefer wired mice (yes, I said "mice"). The additional tools I get from the software for the G502 allow me to customize the G502 far more than I can with either the Master 2 or 3 (both use the same software). With dual monitors, the G502 creates for a seamless work environment. I no longer game, and still the G502 reigns supreme in my hand.

The Master 2 I received gratis from work. It was an arduous request to grant, but eventually my employer succumbed. However, I was far from impressed. I have small-ish hands for an adult, and found the Master 2 too large for comfort. I use a hybrid claw grip, and felt the Master 2 to be a ball in my hands.

But the Master 3 is a worthy upgrade that I recommend to those who are in the similar boat as me. To me, the Master 3 leveled some of that bump; now it contours comfortably to the shape of my palm. The wheel is *excellent*; while I haven't given up on my G502 wheel, I became accustomed to the Master 3 wheel faster than I did to that of the Master 2. I love the mixture of textile plastics on the Master 3. The portions that touch the palm have a rubber-like feel, while the rest comprises a harder feel.

My only qualm is the back and forward buttons. They aren't where my thumb seems to want to find them, and oftentimes I miss pressing them.

Nevertheless, this is my go-to mouse at home.

title: Pretty decent starter projector.
review_text:
We've used this primarily during the lockdown. During the summer, we were able to bust this out for at-home theater. It's not a bad projector by the cost alone, but it's not good enough. This is my first personal projector, and my experience comes from working much more expensive projectors at work.
The projector comes with a storing case, flimsy tripod, remote, and cables. The power cable is very short. If you're using this outside, be prepared to use an extension cable, even if you have an outdoor outlet near. The remote is fine, but most controls can be accessed on the projector. The tripod is very unstable. Even though it's metal, it feels very brittle and I never trust the tripod alone. With a bump, the project can move quite a bit. I therefore use a couple of books for stability.

The projector's zoom features are nonexistent; to create a smaller or bigger picture, you need to manually move the device. Not too bad, but there's a lot of fiddling around. The focus is okay; it doesn't have wide range, but we usually can find a sweet spot pretty quickly. So far we've had success connecting a Chromecast and phones, and therefore are able to watch anything that streams. The picture quality is pretty good, and seems to be right around 1080p. We've never had trouble watching anything or felt that something from the picture was out of focus. Colors seem to be adequate. There are also speakers on this thing, but, as expected, they're not very loud. Thankfully there's a 3.5mm audio jack, which we've used for external speakers.

title: Very easy to assemble. A few quibbles.
review_text:
This is our first projection screen, and we used it quite a bit this summer. It's very easy to assemble on the metal frame. It comes with legs, but we never used them; instead, we posted the screen on the back of the house.
The instructions are straight-forward; after the second assembly and disassembly, we got the hang of it very quickly and didn't need the instructions. The bag it comes with fits everything snugly, and there's even a pouch just for the screen so that it doesn't mix with the metal.
There is a very strong odor when we opened the box. Definitely has a marine smell, but it did go away after the third use.

The screen latches onto the metal frame by buttons. However, the corners are very difficult to snap on, so much so that we decided to leave them unbuttoned. Thankfully there is a surplus of buttons, so the screen stayed straight and wrinkle-free. Even with the screen folded during storage, we didn't notice any creases while watching movies in the backyard. A great investment, especially during the quarantine.

title: Fantastic battery life.
review_text:
These are my first wireless ear buds. I've got a couple of $100+ IEMs, the Sony WH-1000X M3, and Audio-Technica over-the-ear headphones. I think I've got a good sense of under-$500 sound quality, and these Technics are slightly overpriced in my opinion, but they still sound fanstastic.
I have smaller ear canals than normal (as told by my audiologist), so I always opt for a size down when trying on tips. I followed the instructions to insert these Technics buds into my ear holes with the smaller tips, and they fit great. They don't come out with vigorous head-shaking, and haven't come out during my work commutes. I walk about half an hour a day, and so far so good.

The ear buds pair easily, and they always connect to my phone when I take them out of the case. I tried the noise-canceling, but found it to be sub-par compared to my Sony headphones. Sony actually sucks out the volume outside; these Technics add a white noise filter, which to me obstructs the audio I'm listening to. There's an app you can download to your phone which turns off the white-noise filter, so I did that, and turned of equalizer settings. On my phone I use Poweramp v3, AntennaPod, and Amazon Prime HD. They all sound great, but, because the Technics don't slide all the way into my ear, some of the bass gets lost. Higher volumes help, but then you run into ear damage.

Overall, I'm pleased with my first set of wireless ear buds. While they won't take over my Shure IEMs, they're super convenient to have during my work commutes.

title: Sound great, but maybe not perfect.
review_text:
With the right tips, these sound fantastic. I can imagine with further "break-in" and maybe some customization, they will be phenomenal. They are a little bass-heavy, but nothing too detrimental.

For reference, here's what I used:
- Samsung Note8
- VE Odyssey HD DAC
- Poweramp v3
- songs ripped from CD into FLAC using EAC

Here's my previous experience:
- 1More Quad
- Audio Technica ATH-M50x
- Sony WH-1000MX3
- Technics EAH-AZ70W

These sound better than the Technics, but not nearly as good as the Sony. With that said, these wired headphones aren't exactly the best spokesperson for staying wired. I'm all for wired for both audio and video, but I admit that wireless options like the Sony and Technics make me a believer. With the right codecs and setup, you can achieve wonderful results.

There is supreme comfort with these IEMs. With the right tips, I got them fitting snugly in my ear (but there is some trial with error), and there is a metal right around the ear to allow the wire to stay in place. But I question whether these IEMs are worth the price. For $300 you can get cheaper IEMs (imported) with better tips and cables and still have some change in your wallet. And with the push into wireless around the same price range, Shure really needs to push their technology and rely less on their name. Their name alone certainly commands attention, but the wallet is stronger.

title: When it connects, it's great.
review_text:
I have a love/hate relationship with this device. On the one hand, it works great when it actually connects, but on the other hand I hate when it doesn't. It comes with a USB 2.0 dongle, but the keyboard can be very fidgety when connecting to the dongle. I also tested this on a MacBook Pro, but only the mouse feature was tested (which works great).
I'm not sure if it's the battery or the keyboard, but it has a hard time staying connected. I'll lose key presses or the battery will die quickly. It becomes very upsetting when I'm resetting or entering a password and, on Raspbian, I can't see the password due to security measures, so I'll never tell if the keyboard entered the intended keys correctly until I get a success or failure. Usually when I miss a password it's due to user error, but when I'm using this keyboard it can be either user or device error.

The size of it is comfortable in the hand, and the tactility of the buttons feel great. But I feel the size is too small for it to be used as a keyboard comfortably. Some keys aren't placed in standard US ANSI layouts, and the thumb has to do quite a stretch when entering some characters or commands.

title: Excellent general electronics organizer.
review_text:
I carry around with me various cables and chargers, as well as adapters and SD cards. I used to use a roll-up organizer, but found them to be sub-optimal. I also tossed in some cable ties, even though they don't really fit anywhere. But they haven't moved around despite my moving items in and out.

The case isn't hard-shell by any means, but it does do a good job retaining its shape in my backpack. I feel it can protect my goods good enough; by adding smaller chargers in the inside spine, it helps give it a sturdier feel by adding a backbone to the spine.

title: Stays cool. Slow at boot, but speeds up.
review_text:
I'm currently using this with my NextcloudPi setup to store my own data over the network. The Raspberry Pi4 supports USB 3.0, which this SSD also does. That's one of the main things I look for when hounding an SSD: fast transfer rates, as well as large capacity.
I know Samsung has a good reputation for SSD storage; I was very excited when this came in the mail. After re-installing NextcloudPi, I let the setup wizard reformat the Samsung T7 into Btrfs. The T7 formated flawlessly, and the storage shows up completely on both my web panel and my web settings.

I had to restart my Pi4 a few times, and each time I shot some items to my SSD for testing. I noticed it was pretty slow on boot, but after a few hours it seemed to read and write almost as fast as my previous SSD. I supposed, over time, it will adjust to the Pi4. My previous drive was a Verbatim USB SSD, also 3.0. That thing got HOT. It was also made of aluminum on the outside, and I was afraid this T7 would be the same. So far so good; it remains much cooler than the Verbatim.

title: Not sound-proof, but good enough for office use.
review_text:
I knew right away that these would be my office headphones. I have a mechanical keyboard that I use at work, and the office I work in is semi-open. There's a *lot* of noise coming every-which-way. These are a much-needed accessory to my work productivity, as I'm easily distracted by things in my periphery, whether visually or auditory.

The presentation is great. The box is very high quality, reminiscent of the recent Samsung Galaxy device boxes. A smooth matte feel with gloss--weirdly pristine. The box slides out of the slipcover and you get the headphones already in the case. What I like is that they're folded, and there's even a little sheet underneath the phones that always reminds you how to put them back in. Also included is a 3.5mm cable in case you don't want to use Bluetooth, a charging cable, and an adapter. The case is nice, but as I keep mine at work I can't testify to its durability. There's a thin mesh net on the backside in case anyone needs to store one or two thin headphone accessory/-ies along. The accent colors are a nice light copper/rose gold color. I love that color; I'm glad it's getting more attention in recent years.

It didn't take long to charge the headphones, so they come with a little bit of juice. As soon as you turn them on, you get a soft beep along with a voice indicating they're turned on. Nice responsive feedback. Once I put them on I could hear the headphones working to drown out the sound; there was a thick veil of soundproofing that was draped over my ears as soon as the earpads touched them.

The first thing I did was listen to podcasts through the Pocket Casts app and .flac music through Poweramp v3. With podcasts, the difference was phenomenal. Listening to "Wait, wait... Don't tell me!" made me feel as though I were in the audience. The music was fantastic...until I tried on my other headphones which I use for music only.
I thought the bass might've been too strong with the Sony headphones, and I was right. After using even "cheaper" headphones like the Audio-Technica M50x, I could tell the Sony had too much bass. I'm not sure if that's partly because of the noise-canceling technology or what, but the bass can be toned down a bit, methinks.

I then proceeded to download the supplementary app to get the fullest suite of attributes the headphones can get. The app works well, and I didn't experience any hiccups while actually using the app. The only hiccup was when I was trying to download the update. It took *forever*. Almost an hour and it was just halfway through. I decided to bring them to work the next day and let the app sit there while updating. Thankfully, it remembers the progress, even though the app kept crashing during the update process.

There are some optimization tweaks in the app, some sound profiles to let you configure the noise cancelation level (yes, level; the noise cancelation is pure software; you can set it to drown out the most noise as possible or have no noise cancellation at all), and even a little snippet of what is currently playing through the headphones. A simple UI with all the features you need.

The first few days I used it I was active, and I kept noticing that my ears sometimes would pop depending on whether I sat down or arose quickly. Another weird thing is that when I take the headphones off, my ears sometimes need a minute or two to adjust. There's so much noise in the world! After taking the headphones off I can hear HVAC activity and my loud work neighbor who's otherwise not that loud.

I had some headphones with some touch controls before and always found them tacky. I used them once when I first got them and never again. But with these headphones, I'm always using the tap gesture to play/pause and the swipe gesture to raise or lower the volume. There are also swipe gestures to skip or go back a track, but since I never do that anyway I never use those gestures. You have to be careful with the tap; when it works, it works. But the whole surface isn't the active portion and you have to hit it right in the center. Sometimes I'm hitting my finger against my ears trying to find the spot and hurting myself in the process. I tested the gesture where you put your entire palm on the cup to turn off the noise canceling feature and let the mic allow incoming conversation, but not after the third try. I could hear the other people just fine, but I found the right hand over my ear felt awkward, and one person didn't realize I could even hear them. Putting your hand over your headphones isn't a gesture people immediately see as you paying attention to them.

The headphones are extremely lightweight and comfortable to use; I left them on for about two hours once before having to take them off. I actually was surprised with how light they were; when I got the Amazon box I didn't believe it was my headphones. It was much lighter than expected.

For my first noise-canceling headphones I'm pleased. The sound balance can be better (less bass), but they make for fantastic headphones to use at work. I wasn't sure what I was expecting with noise-canceling technology. I thought it would drown out all noises, but you still can hear the occasional mutter; it just won't be distinct.

Oh, forgot to mention the battery life. I charged it only once and have been using it for a week, at about an hour or two each day. Still going well. If you press the power button once it will tell you the battery level. AFter the initial update the voice indicator might give the wrong battery level (it did for me), but give it about ten or fifteen minutes to adjust and it will go back to normal.

title: Swell briefcase. Works fine with my 13" MBP.
review_text:
Now that I'm transitioning to a more corporate world I figured it's about time I get a more "professional"-looking carrying satchel than my Osprey backpack. The only laptops I possess range around thirteen inches, as I find carrying anything heavier than that is far too large to be considered portable.

This briefcase has it all. There are pockets galore; at times I feel there are too many as I keep unzipping the wrong pocket or can't remember in which pocket I put something, so I wish the tags would've been different somehow. Maybe have some lanyards on some or another.

But inside the pockets you get even more pockets and sashes to separate compartments. The material is sturdy and has held up just fine in this insane Chicago spring weather. We've had temperatures ranging from 40-80 in just two weeks, as well as rainy and dry weathers. Chicago, I tell ya!
My 2010 13" MBP fits fine in the main laptop sleeve without sliding around much, and I'm not able to feel much wait on my shoulder from carrying it around all day, along with a couple of books, a Hobonichi planner, and my pencil case.

The main flaw I will say this has is the shoulder strap. It's not easily adjustable, and I still haven't fully figured it out. There is a buckle in the middle on either side--one static, and the other adjustable. But the adjustable buckle doesn't allow the strap easy give, and so I can't for the life of me get it to a comfortable length.
The removable strap is sturdy otherwise.

The other issue is the clasp holding the two handles together. It's not long enough, so instead of closing it with one hand I'm having to use both hands to squeeze the handles together before being able to snap the button together.

All in all, it's a great briefcase usable even with 13" laptops, but the shoulder strap and the handle clasp need better, user-friendly improvements.

title: Great.
review_text:
Since we mounted our TV we like to use as few chords as possible. This way they are neatly tucked along the wall and down into the entertainment center where all our entertainment equipment is housed. So the main HDMI cable runs down but of course we have more components that require a cable than the one connected to the TV. Our solution? A signal splitter. Thankfully, we have only three output connections so this one seemed perfect. Plus, it touts 4k signal, even though most pre-4k HDMI boxes should be fine, but it's nice to have that in the title just in case.

What I use this mostly for is the cable box and a couple of video game systems. As for the cable box, seems to work fine; no dropped signals that I've noticed, nor any degradation in quality. As for game consoles, I have the PS3 and the Wii U hooked up to it. SAme: no noticeable quality degradation nor input lag.
Now, to put it to the real test, I hooked up some retro consoles that have been modded to output native HDMI; that means they'll be HDMI with no lag. Considering I have this and two HDMI cables connecting the console to the TV, I was curious to see if there truly was any lag.
With older games, timing is everything, especially on the 8-bit consoles with platformers and fighters, like the NES. From what I could tell, there was absolutely no lag, not to mention signal loss. The buttons responded as though I were using a normal NES on a CRT.

So yeah, I'm pretty satisfied. It's a bit light and doesn't have heavy pads on the bottom to prevent it from sliding around. With so many cables, and the ability to use the remote control, it should be a bit more stable on the surface.
I haven't used the remote as the detections are instant. No need to manually switch the inputs, at least from my experience. Also, I didn't need to use the power adapter; the power from the HDMI cables seemed to be sufficient, and the detection was not complicated by the lack of adapter. Weird.

title: Basic mount. Tilt is very minimal. No instructions included.
review_text:
Got this to mount a 42" Samsung TV onto our bedroom wall. It is very basic and doesn't require too much knowledge if you've mounted TVs before, but mine didn't come with instructions. I looked online and there are no available instructions, so I had to figure it out from similar mounts and reviews online. The only biggest problem I had was with the screws; I didn't know what width I needed to drill a pilot hole as many PDFs online had different numbers, but I found the right size and drilled away.
Unfortunately, the drill I have wasn't strong enough to drill these all way, but I was able to use a socket wrench to finish putting them in by hand.

The mount is decent, but, again, instructions would've been helpful. For instance, I couldn't tell if the spring-loaded bolts at the bottom of the mount, once the TV is hoisted up, were to be tightened after positioning the TV or left alone. I tried tightening them only to realize they were to be left alone. About five minutes wasted.
I tilting the mount more but really you get about a half-inch's worth of movement.

Otherwise, fine. Fantastic for the price, and more of a fixed mount if you need it.

title: Good watch; buttons a bit hard to press.
review_text:
I run during the summer and run outside. I hate carrying heavy items with me, like water bottles and phones. I feel they sort of hinder my performance, though I realize it's probably more psychological than physical.
Still, I'm not going to mess with a run I've been accustomed to for nearly twenty years, but I do wish, more often than not, that I had some way of tracking my run and how many miles I've done *exactly* while being outside. Sure, I can track the mileage by checking my phone before and after, but it would be nice to have a tracker on me without adding any psychological weight. I used to have a Polar watch that worked fine, but it died some time ago and I never bothered to get a replacement.
But finally I did.

With this one, I'm able to wear the watch without toting my phone along and it still carries all the features and tracking as if the phone were connected to any other tracking watch. While this watch is used for a number of cardio activities, I use it only for running. There are "pages" of exercises you can track, but for a quick run the default is set on the bottom left button--very nice to have, especially for me. Not sure if you can change the default on there to another exercise, but for me it's perfect and I haven't bothered looking up how to change it.
But curious to check out the full features, I ventured into the different pages (or screens) the watch has to offer. During my course, I found that the buttons were *very* stiff. This might be to prevent accidental presses during exercise, but I found that I had to press almost twice has hard as other electronic watches for the watch to recognize my press. But, from my uses so far, I've pressed it mostly to view all the screens when testing out all the features. When actually running, I do no more than a few presses before and after each run. The network had trouble activating itself in the beginning, but that's because I was fiddling with it outside. It kept trying to set itself numerous times when I actually ran outside, but I always dismissed it. Once, however, I was under the open sky I let it connect and it has had no problem or delay connecting ever since.

After every run I am able to sync it with the Epson app, as well as RunKeeper. People have complained about the Epson app but I find it neat and useful.

Overall, it's a great little watch that accurately records my runs and uploads them without the use of the phone during the workout. I'm able to review it speedily on my phone right after, and I love that I can now track my progress without the burden of added weight. It's pricey for sure, but considering I don't need my phone and my previous watch lasted me ten years, I'm sure this watch will be a great investment that will last me hopefully for another decade or so.

title: Pricey, but fits and feels great.
review_text:
We have had a couple of MBPs before getting this one, and those two have sustained minor injuries over the last 10+ years. But since this MBP will be used between two people this time, we decided to get some sort of protection for it besides the padded sleeve. This one was far more expensive than others, but I love the colors and that I could see a majority of MBP. It snaps-fit into the MBP. They're a bit stiff and the snap sounds like it damages the computer, but obviously it's supposed to protect it I guess that's normal.

The kit comes with two filters that fit over the MBP as well, in case you're worried about having full coverage. Though I"m not sure if there are any films to remove from them; they come with tabs that you have to remove--like from phone screen protectors--but they remove nothing when I remove them. I lifted them up and out and just the tabs took off. Weird.

It's very pricey for what it is, but it looks sleek and doesn't add much bulk. I like the blue accents in the inside, though they're barely noticeable when on the computer.
The bump at the bottom where you rest your thumb when using the track pad takes some getting used to. I've been used to the groove of the MBP for years, which has been improved with each subsequent model, but this one tries to make it easier to find the notch but at the same time throws me off because I'm not used to it.

It's a nice case; maybe a bit pricey, but I love the colors. Just wish the Thule logo was more subdued.

title: Great sunglasses; okay smartglasses.
review_text:
As sunglasses, they are phenomenal. They even fit my slightly narrow face. I own a pair of Gascans that I've had for almost eight years and they are my favorite pair of sunnies. Wanted something now that I'm starting to run more and the sun can sometimes cause a harsh glare.
So nice sunglasses with the ability to track my exercises? Sure; why not.

As sunglasses they fit a bit loose on my head, but with the same material that I used on my Gascans I was able to make them tighter by fitting some foam on the hinges; this way they wouldn't (and didn't) loosen while running.
They fit great and are an excellent addition to my running routine. The sun isn't as vibrant as of this writing, but I will continue to use these throughout the winter as the sun's glare on the snow will be an issue.

I tried these on without the smart devices enabled at first to get an idea as to how the sunglasses were by themselves. The box comes with all the electronics apart from the glasses, and the glasses come in a nice semi-hard shell with the additional lens inside. I then equipped everything in one bout.

The earphones fit okay, but they did tend to slide out at times during the few times I've used this so far while running. No issue in terms of when I'm in the gym, however. Syncing from my phone has never been an issue, though I hate carrying it with me.

As smartglasses, they're okay; nothing revolutionary, and it's up to you if you want to pay the premium price for something your phone already can do, provided you take it with you. As the coach doesn't do as much as I'd like as of this writing, as I already have most of my workouts set. I suppose it may not be entirely geared for me as the only exercise I do outdoors is running; the rest is all in the gym.

The music does tend to cut in and out, and I wound up just shutting it off completely after a while. I may look into more comfortable replacements, too.

As sunglasses, these are phenomenal. The perfect sunnies for triathlons, methinks (when they're not wet). But as for smartglasses, a novel idea but needs improvement.

title: Great tablet for the price.
review_text:
For $80, this tablet is actually pretty good. It's about the same height as my Note8, but almost double the width. Still, the tablet-exclusive apps on the Google Play Store work without issue on it, though of course you're going to sacrifice some viewing due to the smaller scale.

When I got the tablet I knew it wasn't going to be anything spectacular. At $80, I knew it wasn't going to compete with the devices I was used to, but it still was nice to have to act as a tablet to play my tablet-exclusive games on and for the kids to use to play their games. The screen of course isn't the sharpest, and out of the box it isn't as sensitive in all areas. Two of the first games I installed were a couple of pinball apps, and the screen had a hard time detecting my presses on the left side.

The screen is quite sharp considering it's a "low-end" tablet, and the feel is very solid. Has a nice textured back to it which makes me reconsider if I'll get a case. The screen does retain fingerprints easily but a quick wipe on a shirt resolves all issues.

There is a microSD slot which is a nice addition; I can transfer any transferable games to that since this tablet has only 16 GB (less considering there's only 14.-something and some of that is taken up by the OS).

Operating the OS is super sluggish. Takes four times as long to do something as it would on a beefier device. But actual in-app operations aren't as bad. A little more sluggish than on a beefier device, but not enough to notice that much.

Since this tablet doesn't have a phone speaker at the top, the actual main speaker is located in its stead. As a result, you get a nice, loud, crisp sound whenever you watch a movie or play a game.

All in all, a fantastic little tablet for the price; I hope the missing sensitivity spots are temporary. The screen isn't as smooth as others, but I'm willing to forgive that for the price.

title: Beautiful watch, but notifications don't always appear.
review_text:
First time using a hybrid smartwatch. I have used fully fledged smartwatches before, but never a hybrid. I was curious as to how they worked. Did they have a mini screen? Did they play notifications? Or was it just a simple vibration gimmick and time and date were synced to the phone? (Answers: #3.)

Anyway, when I got the watch I was impressed right as soon as I opened the box. It was and is beautiful. I love a rose gold tint when it's more copper than pink. Really, many of the rose gold colors geared for men is more of a copper color; not sure why companies are naming them "rose gold." It sounds nicer? Going with the Apple trend? I dunno.
Either way, I like it.

The strap is made of premium leather. I own many leather watch straps, and I love the way this one feels. Light, but solid and soft. The rose gold accentuates it handsomely.

Now, on to the device itself, which, as I stated, is my first hybrid smartwatch.
I have a Note8, and so I've used only an Android to pair with this watch. I don't recall if the box states it works with iOS (I've placed the watch in my drawer and the box is stored in the basement, so I don't feel much like fetching it), but with Android it works fine. I say fine because I did experience some small hiccups which I will discuss further.

The instructions included were bare, but really you're to install the app on your phone and follow the instructions from there. In the quick-start menu you'll get the watch running in less than a minute. The hands move as you set the watch, and everything is synchronized correctly.
The app does all the work for you; you can assign shortcuts to the buttons on either side of the crown, set the notification functions, and so on. For me, I set the upper one to check the alarm and the crown to check the date.

The watch is beautiful on the wrist. I like to wear it with warmer, redder colors, and it fits beautiful with the entire ensemble. The time so far has always been synchronized, but I have noticed some slight hiccups while paired with my phone.

The notifications don't always show. I have one contact set to my favorites, and that one always shoes (both hands move to 1 and the watch vibrates when I get a call or text from the favorite, and subsequent favorites will be moved to 2, 3, etc.). However, I do not always get notifications for texts from others. From my understanding, the watch is supposed to vibrate for texts and calls, even if they're not part of your favorites, but I get notifications almost always just for my favorite, and not the others. I don't recall any notification for an incoming call, whether from my favorite or others.

As a hybrid smartwatch, I like that I can see my steps through the complication, and see the date and alarm settings (though I hate that the date isn't a complication; instead you have to assign on of the three buttons to check the date). However, because it doesn't always detect notifications I'm still perplexed as to utilizing its full functionality. I hope it's just some sort of glitch that will fix itself with...time.

title: Excellent headphones at this price point.
review_text:
Got these for my daughter to use when she has screen time with the iPad or one of our phones. They come in a very nice box with a window display inside the front flap. Included inside were the micro-USB charging cable and the 3.5mm-3.5mm headphone jack--both made of threaded fabric. Very nice.

title: Amazing IEMs with a couple of noticeable drawbacks.
review_text:
I am not an audiophile by any means. I have Rockbox installed on my iPod video classic with a FiiO amp attached, all loaded with FLAC tunes. I listen to Spotify at work. That's the extent of my musical needs.
I have Audio-Technica headphones, and dream of some day owning custom Kaisers. That's my background.

I was pretty excited to get these. Right after ordering, I watched a few YouTube videos on them, and read up on Head-Fi. For the price, 1More seems to deliver outstanding products. Needless to say, I was pretty excited.

The box finally came and I was found to be very impressed with the presentation. You get a nice, magnetic box housing the IEMs, a leather(ette?) pouch, and multiple choices of ear piece tips. For starters, I found that the ear piece tips pre-attached to the IEMs were the most fitted for me, but I still do not find them perfect. They slide down a bit when in my ear, so there is some loss of sound. I will have to buy some aftermarket ones.

The microphone is also sub-par. This is the first time I've used a mic with headphones, and most of my calls could not catch my voice properly. I would get complaints that I sounded muffled or far away, and so I've resorted to using the phone mic most of the time. The mic buttons work flawlessly for playback features, however.

As for the sound, it's fantastic. With four drivers, I can hear so much more--and so many more flaws! I usually transfer music files into FLAC, and so I have pretty good sources for music. I've been using both my Samsung Galaxy S5 and Rockboxed iPod Video (equipped with a Fiio E11), and the sounds are great, but I'm noticing some files that weren't transferred correctly. I cannot connect to my computer speakers at work as the speakers do not have enough power to juice up the Quads, so be sure you have a more recent device or one with enough power to drive these IEMs.

I also use them on my Wii U's GamePad for Breath of the Wild, and they're actually better than my Audio-Technicas, even with the sliding ear tips. I hear a lot more, and sound is very important in the game.

All in all, amazing value for the price. The ear tip issue is more personal as my ears simply don't fit perfectly any of the ones provided, but I do wish the mic worked better.

title: Great Bluetooth headphones, but annoying volume beep.
review_text:
I really like these headphones. The presentation of the setup is done really well, especially considering I've never heard of this brand before. The box comes in a sleeve which removes easily, and the box separates to reveal a lower portion which doubles as a headphone stand. That's really neat! Though I won't use it as I prefer a more dedicated headphone stand, I think it's nice of them to offer it; you can even fish a charging cable through a hole so that it can charge while it's standing.

Comfort-wise, the headphones are really comfortable. I was able to find a good height with them on my head and had no discomfort after wearing it for over an hour.
I had no issues connecting to my phone right away. I have an S5 and it picked up the headphones almost instantly.
I was not able to connect it via my Samsung smart TV, but that may be due to the TV's limitations rather than the headphones'.

The sound is very good, and, despite being wireless, there is no noticeable lag. When I say lag, I mean hearing the playback while monitoring the pace of the playback on the screen.

Now, for the touch controls. Overall, they work really, really well. I think the design of the track-skip and volume is gaudy and detracts from the overall aesthetic of the headphones (for being black, these headphones are otherwise a real eye-pleaser).
However, I did notice on mine that the volume doesn't go very high, and that there's actually a very loud beep whenever I hit max, and it's actually really, really abrasive on my ears. At first I thought it was a one-time thing, but it keeps happening whenever I want to raise the volume and I think it's not loud enough, only to find that I'll reach max pretty quickly.

Otherwise, they're great headphones, connect flawlessly, and are very comfortable. I think the right earpiece, which contains the touch area for track navigation and volume, is a bit tacky and detracts from the aesthetic, but that's a personal preference.
