title: Big fat bass
review_text:
Being a lady approaching that certain age, my ears are not of the necessary construction to accommodate ear buds with any degree of comfort. Indeed, even the increasingly complicated act of bending at the waist can cause regular buds to become dislodged, so I approached these with some measure of reservation.

The memory foam did not feel much different to regular buds, but were not as reluctant to stay put as rubber buds. The construction is good, and the aesthetics are good, but still, they tend to hurt my ears after using them for a while.

I like the cloth covered cord, which feels a whole lot tougher than regular cords; and also the anti-tangle slider which works fine for me, but can be reduced in seconds to a tangled mess in the pocket of my ten year old son.

The big fat bass tends to overpower the higher frequencies a bit, but is still an improvement on other similarly priced models, especially as I prefer heavier bass over tinny trebly sound.

One minor improvement would have been if it had shipped with a case to store the extra buds which tend to get misplaced, and help with my son's tangling issues.

title: Up close and personal
review_text:
I bought this lens to do portraits and general low-light photography, and don't regret it for a minute. It looks a little stunted on the Nikon D7000 after taking off the telephoto, but is a dream to carry around and a snap to use.

Paired with the [[ASIN:B001BTG3OQ Nikon SB-900 AF Speedlight Flash for Nikon Digital SLR Cameras]], anyone can take a picture perfect portrait, and you can capture gorgeous bokeh and snap away in low light situations thanks to the large 1.8 aperture. For the beginner, this lens can autofocus, but you can also switch to manual if preferred. As it is a prime lens, you have to move around to compose your shots (no lazy zooming in) but if you want full body shots, you'll have to move back quite a bit so as not to cut off heads or feet. Same goes for group shots - this isn't an ideal lens for large groups of people.

Included is a lens hood, manual and sturdy drawstring carrying case. For the price, weight and what it can do, this lens is highly recommended for portraits, low-light, general and street photography.

title: A pocketful of everything
review_text:
Pros:

1. A bag big enough to carry all your camera bits and pieces. There's a padded lower compartment with customizable Velcro edged dividers for camera and lenses, a drawstring upper compartment for your what-nots that can be converted to one big compartment with the lower one; five smaller external zippered or Velcro-closing compartments; two pull-out side pouches for water bottles or tripod; a rain cover, and a lot of hooks, straps and loops for attaching gear outside of the bag.

2. The bottom compartment can easily hold a DSLR camera with two or three lenses, or one lens and a flash, or a combination thereof.

3. Smaller pockets have zips &/or Velcro closures for securing lens cleaners, filters, diffusers, spare batteries, chargers, memory cards, remotes or shutter cables etc.

4. Sturdy construction and nicely padded adjustable straps.

5. Cool National Geographic logo to give the impression that you may actually have something to do with the magazine.

Cons:

1. It's a big bag to lug around, especially if you're not built like a rugby player.

2. Even though it's a big bag, and has many pockets, it's still not ideal as a carry-on travel bag, as the upper drawstring compartment is too small to hold a change of clothes and toiletries, and the sideways slit pocket is awkwardly designed to fit a full-sized laptop.

3. It's not possible (or very difficult) to whip out the camera at short notice without taking off the backpack.

4. Too many external loops and fasteners add to the weight.

5. You may have a hard time remembering which pocket you put specific items in.

I use this bag for events or outdoor shoots where I may need more than the basic equipment. For daily use, the [[ASIN:B000YIWNUS Lowepro Fastpack 100 (Red)]]is much more convenient to fetch around.

title: Idiot proof (Using on Nikon D7000)
review_text:
Using this shutter release is so easy that even a beginner like me had it up and running in less than one minute. I've never used one before.

I'm using it on a Nikon D7000 to shoot long exposures, and hope one day to capture a heavenly lightning show without getting electrocuted in the process.

This product has only four components - shutter release button, shutter release button lock, cord and plug. You simply make sure that the camera is turned off, insert the plug end into your camera's accessory terminal and turn on the camera. Remember to turn off the camera when you're done before disconnecting the plug.

Pressing the button (there's only one) is just like pressing the shutter button on your camera, except that you can slide the button to the locked position, go have a cup of tea, and come back and release it to complete the photo. (I exaggerate, but I guess you COULD have a cup of tea if you were doing an extra-long exposure.) The D7000 offers exposures up to 30 seconds, but if you use this handy gizmo, you can scroll past that to "bulb" mode and keep that sucker open to your heart's content.

You can also use it for portraits, self-portraits and for those times when you really want to minimize camera shake. The only problem with the self-portraits is that the cord isn't that long, so you'll probably only get extreme close-ups. If self-portraits are your thing, better get a wireless remote. The one made by Amazon is pretty darned good.

So, camera, tripod, LED flashlight and this wired remote, and I'm all set for some light painting. This is definitely an essential part of any camera gear collection.

Amanda Richards, December 8, 2011

title: Not a whole lotta shaking going on
review_text:
This remote works perfectly with a Nikon D7000, and reportedly will also work with Nikon models D40, D40X, D50, D60, D70, D70S, D80, D90, D3000, D5000 AND D9000 Digital SLR cameras.

It comes with frustration free packaging (albeit too much packing material) and once you remove the plastic tab to make the battery connection, you're good to go. The remote itself is a one-button deal, so there's no need for complicated manuals, at least for the remote.

Getting the camera set up for remote shooting is the major challenge, as the Nikon manuals are not easy to follow. It's much easier to do a search on YouTube and follow the videos there.

If you are using the remote to include yourself in family photos, take sneak pics of unsuspecting wildlife or minimize camera shake while taking lights at night or portraits by day, this can be done simply by rotating the camera's release mode dial (on model D7000) which is below the mode dial (the one that says P, A, S, M, scene, U1, U2 etc.) to the second to last setting, putting your camera (and tripod if necessary) where you want it, setting up the shot, and beetling off within a 16 foot radius, pressing the single button when you are ready. That's it.

For long exposures, rotate the release mode dial one more place to the last setting, which is called Mup, or Mirror Up. One press raises the reflex mirror and the second press releases the shutter and resets the mirror. Of course shooting fancy stuff like lightning, star trails and the craters of the moon requires a full knowledge of the manual setting on your camera, a sturdy tripod and a lot of patience, but this remote will do its part of the job with just one button.

If only the manual camera settings were as easy to use as this remote, I'd be a pro in no time flat.

title: Hot flash
review_text:
What looks like a flash, acts like a flash, but is much more than your average flash?

This gadget provides a painless backup solution for businesspersons and students who can't survive without their trusty laptop/netbook/notebook and the information therein. Even for users unfamiliar with backup software, the Echo software included on the drive is a snap to use. Once the backup drive is inserted into a USB port on your computer, it will take you through some simple steps to configure the backup. You can choose the easy predefined Automatic plan or you can choose the more advanced Custom backup plan. There is a Quick Start Guide, also included on the drive, which provides a brief explanation of the options that are available.

When configuring your Custom backup profile, you can specify which file types you want backed-up. You can select ALL files, or there are some basic ones such as text, spreadsheet, presentation, music, videos, photos et al that you can select. There is also an OTHER category where you can define other file types that may be important to you, for example, zip, rar, pdf, etc. In addition, you select which folder(s) you want backed-up, set filters if required, and set the number of versions of files to keep, a useful option if you accidentally delete or modify a file. There is also the option to select an Automatic backup which activates every time you plug in your flash drive, and Live which continuously backs up your modified files to the flash drive without your intervention.

Restoring files is just a matter of clicking on the Restore menu button, selecting the files and/or folders you want restored and setting the location where to restore the files, then hit RESTORE. Alternatively, if when creating your profile, you had decided not to password protect it and encrypt it, the files can be accessed quite easily from directly on the root of the backup drive in the My Backup folder.

To backup another computer, you would have to install the software on that computer and set up another backup profile.

This version of the Lexar Echo has only 16GB of storage capacity, and is really too small to back up more than one home computer with music and video files; it can barely back up one computer, much less two or more. On the other hand, it would certainly be good for business people on the road since they will generally be using smaller files and the backup is a no-brainer.

While it has a good feel to it and the retractable connector saves losing caps, it is a bit on the `chunky' side and competes for space with other USB devices. It can also get damaged if you're not careful when moving the laptop around and it gets hit during the process, as it sticks out quite a bit.

I did not check for backup/restore speeds nor did I follow up on the 2GB of free online backup space which was offered in the setup. It appears this is no longer available at DMAILER, the backup software manufacturer; but instead I was guided to check YuuWaa online backup services.

Extremely handy for business or school use, and especially for people who have senior moments and accidentally delete or write over important files on a regular basis.

title: Not quite spy-gear
review_text:
First of all, the D-Link camera is relatively easy to set up - always the one to play with techie stuff first, my husband had it up and running in a flash (well almost a flash). Just attach the supplied cable to your computer, run the CD and follow the simple instructions and you're good to go. According to the instructions, you have two options to set up the camera: wirelessly or wired. Naturally, my husband tried the wireless option first, which didn't work because it claimed (spuriously, we believe) that it couldn't find the network, so he had to resort to the other method, which worked right away. We're using a Linksys wireless router.

The camera works quite well indoors where the intensity of the ambient light is generally much lower than outdoors. However, in the brighter outdoor light it is difficult to discern what you're looking at (is it a bird, is it a plane?). The colour is not the best, but then again, it ain't a Nikon 7000. There is some amount of adjustment that can be done online to change the settings, but you'll need to create an online account/register your camera first with D-Link at [...] This is also necessary if you want to view your camera remotely. Strange enough, whenever I try to access the camera online, I get a message telling me that the application needs an earlier version of Java. However, after hitting <Run> for the next three dialogue boxes or so that pop up, it will display the picture. I tried accessing the camera from outside my home network but was unable to do so. Maybe firewall issues?? (Too much effort required to check this). There is also an iPod app that is quite good, minus sound.

Night vision was surprisingly good too. In the dark, the images were shades of grey, but in brighter conditions, the colour returned. Four LED lights lit up whenever the night vision was activated (could be an issue if you wanted to place it somewhere discrete).

On the down side, the camera has to be plugged into an electrical socket to work, and the cord it came with is very short. This means you have to either place it near an electrical outlet or use an extension cord. This would obviously have limitations on where you can place it. It also has to be connected to your home network whether wired or wireless.

While in theory it could be used as a security camera, it has to be powered 24/7, so if you live in a country or area prone to an uneven power supply which could damage sensitive equipment, then you may want to consider that before getting it or you may need to install additional equipment such as line conditioners/UPS to protect your equipment.

The sound is not very good. In fact, after a few hours use it started to make a clicking sound in an endless loop.

Recommended for limited applications such as keeping an eye on kids (or pets, or pesky guests), or when you're avoiding (hiding from) certain people who come calling at your gate, but not as a dedicated security system.

title: iLike
review_text:
This review deals with the performance of the iLuv iMM747 Audio Cube using an iPod Touch and an iPad 2.

Pros:

1. Easy to open packaging, easy to set up, easy on the eyes.
2. Slightly big for a bedside table, but a good size for a desk.
3. Convenient controls on the top if using it at a desk.
4. Charges device while in operation.
5. Good quality sound, reasonable bass and volume without distortion.
6. Syncs with iTunes when connected to a network.
7. Easy to dock the iPod Touch.
8. You can watch videos or TV shows using it as a base with big speakers for your tiny touch screen television.
9. Small enough to tote around for big sound at sleepovers or small gatherings.
10. Cooler looking and lighter than a boom box.

Cons:

1. No remote control.
2. No remote control.
3. No remote control.
4. Power cord is too short, and the wall adapter is a bit large for outlets that are close behind bedside tables or other furniture.
5. The iPad 2 is hard to dock due to the angle and placement of the port.
6. The back support is not tall enough to hold the iPad 2 securely, or at least it seems that way to me.

Other:

1. You need to take the device out of the case before placing in the docking station.
2. A message saying "Application not installed" pops up when you power it up, even though all apps are up to date.
3. If you can play Angry Birds sideways, you can get the sound effects at high volume (this may be considered a bad thing)

Conclusion:

Good value for the price, and high quality sound for the size.

title: Love/Hate Relationship
review_text:
As a general rule, I hate hands-free handsets.

I hate it when I begin speaking with someone, and I think they're agreeing with everything I say, and then it turns out they're actually talking to someone else using their dratted ear extension with the flashing blue light.

I hate the fact that my ears are the wrong size and shape for the majority of headsets.

I hate it when my untrained (clumsy) fingers hit the wrong part of the headset when I'm simply trying to stop it from falling to its death from a height of just over 5 feet, and I either redial the last number or hang up on the one person who hates being hung up on.

Plus, they're UGLY, and don't accessorise well with any wardrobe!!

HOWEVER,

I hate it even more when I have to pull over and park to take or make a call.

And I especially hate it if I DON'T pull over, and then get busted by the only policeman on the entire empty highway who has insomnia and a full book of blank tickets waiting to be filled in.

SO,

Hands free it shall be -
But ONLY when I'm driving.

That said, this device fits most of my basic needs, and throws in some convenient extras. The EASYGO Headset was indeed very easy to set up and even easier to use. Sound quality was good and the spoken connection status and audio volume adjuster are useful features.

The headset is also relatively small and stylish (as hands-free headsets go) without any flashing lights or buttons that attract unwanted attention (or cause an attack of photosensitive epilepsy, or signal the letters N-E-R-D in morse code.)

The most impressive feature of this headset has to be the long battery life, which is great because the miserly charger cord is so awkward to use that you don't want to have to use it more often than necessary. Besides, as I only use it in the car, it lasts me several trips, depending on how often and how long I prattle.

Admittedly it is more comfortable to use than I expected. The extra ear hook prevents suicidal leaps from ear to earth, and it doesn't weigh my head down on one side.

In summary, for a simple headset, it delivers.

Rated: 4.5 stars

title: Reasonable expectations
review_text:
When buying a product like this, it's wise not to go into the transaction with great expectations. In my case, this was a risk free trial, having won this item at a games arcade thanks to my considerable skill at spending vast quantities of money to win wonderful prizes such as shot glasses and lop-sided teddy bears.

Howz it work?

1. The machine looks like a CD player (or possibly like one of those cheap rolodex thingies that are made to look like CD players)
2. It comes with one pair of blue topped discs, and a 30ml bottle of liquid for cleaning CDs, DVDs, Game discs and the like.
3. It also comes with one pair of beige topped discs and a 10ml tube of cream for repairing discs.
4. Choose which set of discs you need, press the button to open the lid of the machine, and then insert them in the holes. You'll need to turn each disc until it is securely anchored (rotate it counter-clockwise until it stops)
5. Note that the left side is labeled "Dry" and the right side is labeled "Wet" (It's a bit hard to see if you're not looking for it)
6. Apply the appropriate solution - 4 drops of cleaning liquid or 3 small dollops of repair cream - on to the disc on the "Wet" side
7. Place your disc data side down and close the cover.
8. Plug in the machine (110/120V) and press either the "Clean" button or the "Repair" button on the front of the machine.
9. It will automatically turn itself off when the process is finished. (You won't have any problem knowing when it's done - it makes an awful racket when it's working)

Pros:

1. Dirty and scratched CDs, DVDs, Game discs and the like can be given a new lease on life.
2. Cleaning only takes a minute, and repairing just four minutes.
3. Easy to operate

Cons:

1. Looks cheap
2. The cleaning and repair solutions are supplied in tiny quantities (30ml and 10ml respectively) which are used up in no time at all.
3. Replacement kits of discs and solution are comparatively expensive.
4. Noisy

However:

1. It really worked to repair an extremely scratched PS2 game disc that would no longer play in the system. In just over 4 minutes the game was back in the console and working like new. (Some of the scratches were still visible - apparently the solution forms a coating over scratches)
2. It cleaned dirt and fingerprints from an audio disc without any problems.

title: Mostly kewl keyboard
review_text:
Not being a techie, this review will be based on the experiences of an average Joe or Jane trying this keyboard on for size.

Pros:

1. Excellent packaging. Easy to open, and is packed in a compact and attractive box. Would make a great gift.
2. Nice comfortable palm rest and key positioning. The removable feet required a bit of reading of the instructions to set up, but this was relatively easily accomplished. Note: Be careful you don't throw out the feet with the packaging.
3. Easy set up. Up and running in minutes.
4. Works with batteries, so no need to store and locate a charger when the mouse runs out of steam. (As compared to the Logitech model)
5. Handy buttons for MS Office, such as cut, copy, paste, undo, bold, italic and underline (et al) right on the keyboard. (as dual key functions)
6. Media keys and volume controls on keyboard, also low battery indicator light.
7. Compact footprint, so it can fit most workstations.

Cons:

1. Can you say "dust magnet"? This thing picks up dust and fingerprints like crazy, especially on the shiny bits.
2. Lack of detailed instructions for the keyboard and mouse. It comes with adequate set-up instructions, but expects you to know what to do after that. I'd have appreciated some included info on the keyboard functions.
3. No lights for Caps lock and Num lock
4. Mouse has no on/off switch (that I can find), so when I turned it over and put in the batteries (2 x AA included) I nearly blinded myself with the blue laser. Note: It turns off when the receiver is stored in the base.
5. Mouse is obese. Hard for small hands to deal with, and not ergonomic.

Note:
I don't have Windows 7 as yet, but it's nice to know that whenever I get it, the keyboard has special "hot keys" to allow easy access to programmes.

Overall, a good keyboard/mouse combination for the price, with more positive features than negative if you're an average computer user. I can't speak for Gamers or Techies, but I like it.

title: Badly framed and not well hung
review_text:
If you're looking for an "el-cheapo" digital frame, you may have hit the jackpot with this one. Not only is it relatively low-priced, but it also comes with low quality picture reproduction, low quality sound, and badly thought out button placement.

To be fair, it takes flash drives and camera cards, and plays MP3s and videos and can do slideshows and tell you the time and date.

But...

The power cord makes the whole "hanging on the wall" thing a bit of a joke, the lack of internal memory is a pain I'd rather not have, and the music that comes out of the in-frame speakers certainly isn't the food of love.

The USB cord mentioned in the booklet is not included, so if you don't happen to have one handy you'll have to use flash drives and camera cards for picture storage.

Talking about photographs, this frame will take your 3MB memories and make them look like 70KB internet snapshots, so this may not be a good gift for your favorite photo-take-outerer.

Navigation is tricky and could be a lot easier, and the buttons and doo-dads are awkward to negotiate, especially as the button color blends in with the back of the frame.

I guess you could give this to your dear old Gran, especially if she has failing eyesight and hearing, and you were able to visit her daily to set it up and change the pictures, but in this high-tech world, anyone else would expect much better picture and sound quality.

Economically priced, and not worth the price tag.

title: I do not like them, Sam-I-am
review_text:
I would not, could not,
on a plane.
Not in the park. Not on a train.
Not in a car. Not on CD.
I do not like them, Sam, you see.
Not in my bed. Not on a boat.
Not on my head. Too big to tote.
I will not use them here or there.
I do not like them anywhere!

Pros:

1. Looks and feels like the more expensive models
2. Nicely padded and sturdy
3. Comes with a handy drawstring carrying bag, or you can get the optional hard case, which is extremely durable
4. Folds up much smaller than it looks
5. Comes with an adapter so that two headphones can be connected to the same audio source
6. Comes with a nice long cord, so you can use it at your desktop comfortably
7. Cancels out noise from your surroundings to a certain extent
8. Reasonably priced

Cons:

1. No instructions. However, it only takes minutes to figure out where the battery goes (right side), how it folds and adjusts, and where the cord plugs in. (I had to figure this out right away, because it arrived with the switch in the "on" position and a dead AAA battery)
2. For the noise cancelling feature, the on/off button is located quite inconveniently behind your right ear
3. While it muffles some of the background noise, it still lets through quite a lot, and the hissing noise can bother some users. You can still hear the sound of the keys on a keyboard when you type, but when you take it off there is a noticeable difference. A loud party in the neighborhood became a lot more bearable with them on.
4. As a regular headphone this one is unfortunately not very good. You can hardly hear anything with the noise cancelling feature off, and when you put it on, it manages to remove all the bass resulting in a tinny sound.
5. Even folded, it's still quite bulky to tote around

Conclusion:

Rugged and expensive looking, this headphone promises effective noise-cancelling features and good audio sound.
Unfortunately, it falls short in both categories.
I do not like them, Sam-I-am

Yay: Sleek, smooth, shiny glossy black finish; trim and slim
Nay: Fingerprints!!!

Yay: 60 minutes recording time; HD-Quality video; 4GB memory

Yay: Charges using a USB port. On-screen battery indicator tells you when it needs charging. Charges while you're uploading the day's footage to the computer. Does not use regular batteries or require a separate charger.
Nay: You'll have to make sure it's charged before you leave home if you're not toting your laptop. No chargee, no filmee.

Nay: Not easy if you're using a desktop, particularly when you already have the receiver for your [[ASIN:B001DJ9GOS Logitech Cordless Desktop Wave Pro (920-000919)]] plugged in. I tried using a USB extension cable, but got a message on the display that said it was too hot and had stopped charging.

7. Uploading:

Yay: Just connect to your computer

Yay: All your clips are displayed on the computer screen, and you can edit them to select just the parts you need for your movie. Big Yay: You can fiddle with the background sound, making your added music softer or louder, or taking out the background sound altogether. title: Catch the Wave
review_text:
A keyboard used to be a rather boring, under-appreciated, rectangular attachment to your computer, useful for typing stuff, and for catching stray staples, bits of paper from your paper punch, dust and assorted DNA particles.

Now here comes the Wave Pro, with a sensuous curvy design, and a whole lot of kewl features that you never knew you needed until now. This model comes with an MX1100 Cordless laser mouse, both sharing a common USB micro-receiver.

Features:

Cordless Keyboard

1. Windows Vista Flip 3D button, that helps you to switch between application windows easily. With XP you get a pop up list of your open windows, but with Vista you see your windows in 3D view, and then use your arrow keys or mouse to choose your next destination page.

2. Zoom keys to get that paragraph to a size you can read, even without your progressive lenses.

3. Special Vista keys that bring up all the Vista features, and all your picture files, each with the click of one button.

4. Navigation keys for multimedia - volume, mute, play, pause, stop, fast forward, skip back. This is a very handy feature - kind of like a monster sized remote control

5. One button to bring up your Media Player

6. One button to bring up your Media Center, where you can listen to music, or watch a movie, tune in to the television, view your picture files in a slideshow, check out MSNBC.com and more.

7. Call up a handy calculator in a jiffy

8. Sleep button

9. Fn key to give each of the function keys a second job to do, such as launch Word or Excel, your favorite website, your IM page or e-mail or favorite search engine.

10. Battery status indicator.

11. Contoured keyboard with palm rest for comfortable typing. This design works very well for people who can type with the proper fingers, but also does the job for the two-fingered corn-pickers among us.

12. Displays actions on your monitor for a few seconds so you're less likely to accidentally hit your Caps button without noticing it.

Cordless Mouse

See: [[ASIN:B001DJ64C0 Logitech MX 1100 Cordless Laser Mouse]]
(NB) On its own this mouse uses 2 AA batteries, but when packaged with the keyboard it uses a rechargeable battery.

Cons:
1. The keyboard is pretty big (albeit understandably so) and takes up quite a bit of space on the desk. I'd get around this by typing with the keyboard on my lap and my feet up on the desk, but they tell me it's not good office practice.

2. The mouse uses rechargeable NiMH batteries - good for saving on dead batteries, but a real pain to keep track of the charger, which you'll need once every six weeks.

Conclusion:

The "Ayes" have it - regardless if you're a whizz at data entry or a two-finger wonder, this keyboard makes a lot of functions easier, and the Media Center and handy navigation keys put it way ahead of other keyboards.

Add it to your own Christmas list this year.

Amanda Richards, November 3, 2008

title: `twas the month before Christmas
review_text:
`twas the month before Christmas
And all through the house
There were two creatures stirring -
Just me and my mouse

As I opened the package
I noticed with glee
That the mouse could be freed
And set up easily

Five minutes or less
Was all that it took
To download the software,
Now let's have a look......

First off, this is an expensive mouse, so if you only use the computer to check e-mail and surf the occasional site, you really don't need to splurge on this, except of course if you're going for that professional look.

Next, if you're looking for portability and your laptop bag already fits your laptop rather snugly, you might want to choose a smaller mouse, as this Rubenesque babe will definitely need space to stow her curves. I think it's better suited to a desktop machine. If you like a smaller mouse for toting around the place, or if you have small hands, you may want to try the [[ASIN:B000TKHBDK Logitech VX Nano Cordless Laser Mouse for Notebooks]] instead.

Fit wise, it suits a medium to large hand pretty well, and the buttons are well placed for a right hander, except for the back and forward buttons which will need some thumb flexing practice before you can get used to it.

Feature wise, it has the same hyper-fast and precision scrolling options like some of the other Logitech models, except that now there's a separate button for choosing the settings. The same scroll wheel can be used to move horizontally across documents (like big spreadsheets). You can also adjust the sensitivity using the plus and minus keys on the top left hand side of the mouse.

There's also a cool "hidden" button within easy reach of your thumb that helps you to switch between application windows. With XP you get a rather boring pop up list of your open windows, but Vista makes it possible to have your windows shown in 3D view, and you can use your arrow keys or mouse to choose your next destination page.

Another plus for me is that it uses two regular AA batteries, and has an indicator light that turns red when you have but one week of battery life remaining. I already have far too many chargers and cables and other thingies to be able to keep track of them all, and I really don't need another one to add to the pile.

Overall, this is a good mouse with features worthy of the price, but a bit on the large side. Recommended for right-handed professional desktop computer users.

Amanda Richards, November 3, 2008

title: Are you an "innie" or an "outie"?
review_text:
Some people prefer their headphones outside of their ears, with comfortable ear cushions and other features, such as the [[ASIN:B00007056H Koss KTXPRO1 Titanium Portable Headphones with Volume Control]]. Others prefer wearing their headphones in the privacy of their own ears, with the added bonus of noise isolation.

There are good reasons for choosing either type depending on your personal preferences, such as comfort levels, where and when you're using them, what you're listening to, and whether or not you have to share with other people.

For general use at home, I use the regular "outie", especially for movies or music with inappropriate language that I'd rather not play in surround sound in the presence of young `uns. I also let my son use it when I'd rather not hear another note from the Jonas Brothers. However, in the wee hours of the morning when the only creature stirring is me, I prefer to use in-ear headphones, which shut out everything except the music.

At work, I hardly ever use headphones due to the telephone ringing off the hook, but at lunchtime I sometimes use the in-ear headphones for peace and quiet. I drive to work, so no headphones are needed for the daily commute.

This is a fairly expensive model, but it's worth every cent if you can safely use headphones that cut out most external noise.

Pros:

1. Really nice packaging, easy to open, simple instruction manual
2. Cool, sleek and compact black metal carrying case included, with a cleaning tool and cable clip as accessories.
3. It comes with three different sizes of rubber caps, and as Goldilocks might say, one is for ears that are big, one's for smaller ears, and one will no doubt be just right. Changing caps is simple too.
4. It also includes a pair of memory foam sleeves that fit so snugly in your ears that you may think they belong there.
5. The caps are washable, once you dry them properly before using them again.
6. The sound is marvelous, clear and true, and there's no need to raise the volume to sonic boom levels.
7. The headphones are clearly marked left and right, and are at an angle for easy insertion and a tight seal
8. Drastically cuts down on external noise

Cons:

1. Unless you're using it for an IPod or other portable device, the cord is too short.
2. May feel a bit weird for some people due to the superior noise isolation.
3. You may experience "ewwwwwwwwwww" moments when your friends grab them and try them on. These aren't for sharing.
4. Try saying "in-ear headphones" out loud six times

If you're looking for an excellent pair of (deep breath) in-ear headphones, I think you'll be pleased with this one.

title: I like to move it, move it ....
review_text:
Logitech says that their products are designed to move you, and this mouse sure lives up to that promise. Seconds after opening the beautifully packaged box, I was up and running and you can do it too. The instructions tell you everything you need to know, from how to put in the batteries (2 x AAA, included), how to turn it on (power button on the bottom), and where to insert the Nano receiver (USB port). For more features, Windows users can install the software included, and Mac users can go get the download.

Installation takes quite a few minutes, but once that's over, your mouse gets super powers, and can scroll from side to side (perfect for those extra wide pages), help you search the internet with the push of a button, and also navigate backwards and forwards between internet pages. How cool is that?

Here's all the OTHER good stuff about the VX Nano:

1. It's cordless
2. It's compact and cute, and oh so ergonomic (at least for small hands)
3. The MicroGear Precision Scroll Wheel (fancy name for the wheel thing between the buttons that you scroll with) has two modes: Hyper-Fast, for when you need to scroll down long documents at warp speed, and Ratchet, for when you don't have a long, long way to run. You switch between them by simply pressing down on the wheel. (Tilting the same wheel left or right gives you the side by side scrolling once you've installed the software)
4. There's a LED light to tell you when your batteries need changing
5. There's a compartment at the bottom of the mouse to store the Nano-receiver securely. Alternately, you can just leave the little thing attached to your notebook USB port.
6. The package includes a nice Logitech zippered case to keep your mouse snug as a bug in a rug.
7. You can use it on your desktop machine too. It comes with an "extension cord" that you plug into the USB port of your CPU, and insert the Nano-receiver into the little gizmo at the other end, and you're all set. I didn't even have to evict the regular mouse that was already living on my mouse pad.

Believe me, after you've gone Nano you'll never want to go back to cords again.

title: How to look like a pro (even if you're not)
review_text:
This Targus notebook case is a great way to carry around all your stuff and still look cool, professional and ready for action.

The good stuff:

1. It can fit notebooks up to 17" securely and safely. There's a strap to hold your equipment in place, it's nicely padded and has an adjustable inner wall for extra snugness. It even opens like a briefcase for easy packing.
2. The same compartment has three pockets with Velcro closures, a zippered mesh pocket and some slots for letters, warranty cards or other documentation. There's ample space for a mouse (optical, cordless, furry with tail), flash drives, cds and dvds, cords, headphones, bells and whistles.
3. The zipper for the notebook section can be locked with a padlock.
4. The front flap has an easy fastener, and also has a zip pocket, right at the front of the bag, perfect for passport and tickets when traveling
5. Lift the flap for another compartment, and more pockets, with slots for pens, glasses, keys, and whatever else you like to carry around.
6. The back has a padded Velcro-closing pocket for newspapers, magazines or other reading matter.
7. Yet another zippered compartment has two slots for important documents and not so important documents.
8. The handle is tough rubber, defying you to mess with it, and the bottom and sides are protected with a corrugated rubber strip. You can set this one down on the floor - it can take it.
9. Even if you aren't carrying around a laptop all the time, this case works fine as a large briefcase for work or travel, with lots of room for a change of clothes, product samples, toiletries (make sure they adhere to airline safety regulations), files, manuals, snacks, extra undies and more.

The other stuff:
1. If you have a 17" laptop, there's not enough space in the padded section to hold your power cord, but there are so many other compartments and pockets that this shouldn't pose a major problem - other than remembering where you put it. (There's plenty of space for a bottle of Ginkgo Biloba)
2. It's pretty durn heavy to lug around, especially for those already having to contend with a full handbag, cup of coffee and high heeled shoes
3. The generous number of compartments encourages you to carry around more stuff than you need - just in case of emergencies. (And then of course you can't remember where you packed them in the first place)
4. It tends to fall over if you don't put it down carefully or lean it against something.
5. The strap looks a little cheap compared to the rest of the case, and keeps spinning around, so you always have to check that the padded piece is on the inside, but it's easier to carry it by the handle anyway.

Sturdy, roomy, comfy and a tad bit clunky, but overall a good case for larger notebooks, work or travel.

title: Convenient, but needs careful handling
review_text:
We bought this as a gift for our son, to keep him occupied on long car trips, and while traveling. It is compact and light enough to tote around without breaking your shoulder, and comes with accessories for playing in the car, an AC cable, and also has a rechargeable battery for wireless viewing anywhere. It even comes with a remote (but not a pretty one)

For adults this is a great little gadget - it never gets into a snit over bumpy roads or potholes, and with your headphones on, it can give you hours of viewing when you’d rather be alone. The screen even swivels around for the best possible picture in cramped situations.

For kids however, there are some things you should note:

1. The silver finish gets scratched and dirty quickly

2. The power is controlled by a slider button which doesn’t feel as sturdy as it should – ditto the button to open the section where the DVD goes

3. The button to open the player is right in front where little hands can accidentally press it while in use.

4. On the right hand side, there’s a button to choose the DVD format. This often slides to the other side when taking it out of the case, and fools you into thinking that the player isn’t working.

5. Our video display stopped working on Day 2, until we reset it by unplugging the player without turning it off and then plugging it in again.

6. The control buttons on the player itself are not very user friendly, and I still have no idea what some of them do, but I haven’t needed to use them so far anyway.

7. You can’t play old or scratched discs, as these will damage the player. (I don’t know about you, but most of my kid’s DVDs are scratched and battered)

Picture quality and sound are good, as is portability. Overall, this is a very convenient DVD player for traveling or commuting, but one that requires care and attention to work properly.

title: Light n' Easy
review_text:
The one important thing to note when buying electronic equipment is that once you pop, you can't stop. Every time you think that you have the perfect system, something else comes along that you absolutely HAVE to have, which leads to something else, and so on ad infinitum.

Having bought new surround sound speakers, we needed a new DVD player, and then, naturally, a new receiver. The weight of this system is a big plus, being less than half the weight of our old one, but the new one's not as aesthetically pleasing with those shiny silver buttons.

Leaning over the shoulder of my resident techie, I can now advise as follows:

1. You cannot connect a turntable to this receiver; there are no phono inputs. Not good for those of us who still have LPs.

2. It's DVD-Audio ready for the audiophiles among us.

3. Setup is relatively easy, controlled by two buttons only: a multi control button and the input selector button. This can be irritating if you need to adjust the tone after you have finished setting up, since there are no separate bass and treble buttons, and you have to go through the setup menu again. You can however adjust the level of the surround speakers and subwoofer from the remote.

4. No onscreen display available

5. No switched AC outlets to allow you to plug in other components.

6. In addition to the receiver, the universal remote can be used to control a TV, tape, DVD player/recorder, VCR, CD player and the radio. This reduces the number of remotes you need around you. It has a weird shape that takes some getting used to, and I still use my separate remotes - guess old habits die hard.

7. Input jacks on the front make connecting camcorders, video games, etc. quite easy.

8. When listening to music or looking at a movie, there are SFC (Sound field control) modes which you can choose to enhance the sound environment. For music there are six modes (live, pop/rock, jazz, etc.), and for movies another six (action, drama, sports, etc.) However, to the untrained ear, like mine, I cannot detect a significant difference if any of these modes are selected.

Overall, the sound from this receiver is quite good, very clean, though it doesn't seem as powerful as my old receiver (a Technics SADX930). This could be due to differences in the calibration of the volume control, but since I rarely play it at very high volumes this is a non-issue. The centre channel seems a bit weak compared to the other channels, but with so many sound options to choose from and customize, it is very possible that I may have missed something and need to tweak it some more.

A very nice receiver for the price and features.

Amanda Richards, December 14, 2004

title: A pretty darn good space saving, high performance machine
review_text:
I picked up this little beauty to replace both an ancient and cranky 5-disc CD Player and a single disc DVD player. I now have breathing room in the old entertainment center, so even my antique turntable can take a creaky spin every now and again.

Seeing that I can't connect a toaster without help, I called on my trusty better half to unravel the mystery of setting it up. In non-technical language, a.k.a. plain English, this is what you need to know about this mighty machine:

1. The manual needs a lot of work. It's neither user-friendly nor idiot-proof. Ditto for the boxy silver remote.

2. It is easy to set up if you already know how to do that sort of thing. (We have component video connections to the TV and digital coaxial connections to the receiver.)

3. It gives excellent sound from both CDs and DVDs. With the benefit of 5.1 surround, movies like Master and Commander can literally move you, and CDs have never sounded better.

4. It is as convenient as a 5-disc CD changer as it is a 5-disc DVD player, except that when you're playing more than one CD you'll need to put it in "CD Mode" first.

5. It can easily play different types of media, such as audio Cds, MP3s, DVDs and those other mysterious formats - just put in the discs and play away.

6. The video quality is very good on a regular TV. You can set up different pre-defined picture quality modes, or customize to suit your own taste if you're a techie or a buff. If you have difficulty making up your mind, ignore this option.

7. The player is chock full of options, but you have to explore for yourself, which can be a bit confusing until you get the hang of it. Read the manual, you say? See Item 1 above.

8. There's on-screen information for MP3s and photo CDs, with different views available for the contents. (Groups/folders or entire playlists)

9. I can't comment on the progressive scan feature, since I don't have an HD or HD-ready TV - yet. (Still waiting for that lottery win)

10. It is supposed to play DVD-Audio discs, but you need 6.1 channel inputs on your receiver to play them. Unfortunately, our receiver is lacking these inputs, but then again, I am also lacking any DVD-Audio discs.

Electronics buffs will probably say that it needs a bit of "tweaking" to get it to look and sound just right, but it looks and sounds great to me. All in all a very good player, perhaps excellent when you factor in the price.

Amanda Richards, October 1, 2004

title: Great sound, Great value, Crazy lights
review_text:
I was looking for an inexpensive CD Player for the company car that I drive, and bought this one on the recommendation of the dealer.
The car only has the standard front speakers, so it is a bit of overkill, given the power of this player, but even with the existing speakers it sounds fantastic.
The detachable flip down front panel is a feature that got full marks from my more electronically minded co-workers.
Attaching and detaching the panel requires practice, as it's not that easy to do, especially when you're in a hurry. It's so uncool to have to use both hands to do it, so I'll continue to work on that aspect.
The remote control feature was an added incentive to buy it, and it comes in handy, except when my son gets his hands on it and keeps repeating the same song over and over from the back seat. He's two years old, so that shows how simple it is to use the remote.
It picks up radio signals from miles away, and the increased choice of channels was an unexpected plus.
My major problem with it is the lights. This thing lights up like a Christmas tree, which at night can be distracting. I've heard that you can dim them, but haven't had the time to read the manual to find out how. Until then I just flip down the front panel so they don't show.
Definitely no regrets buying it

title: Nice watch
review_text:
This is my first running watch. Although this is listed as a "Smart Watch", it's only "Smart" when it's liked to your phone.
I use it as a running watch and a fitness tracker and it works great for a beginner like myself.

It has built in GPS which is great for tracking runs and walks. It gives you all the basics like pace, cadence, distance, and time. You can configure the data fields to your liking, change watch faces, and download other apps.

The GPS is very accurate, I compared the distance on the high school track and after 14 laps it was within a few feet of the track distance. An app using my phone's GPS was 1/2 mile off. (My guess is that measuring a distance from one point to another will be easier and more accurate than 14 laps around a 400 meter track.)

The watch screen is optimized for outdoor running and it works great in the sunlight. As it gets darker you need to tilt the watch at an angle to see the screen. I've run at sun up ad sun down without issue. The screen is backlit but you need to push a button. That's a little awkward when your running, but I rarely run in the dark. I have not had any problems seeing the screen indoors with normal lighting.

I picked this watch because of the low profile, large face, and relatively low price as it is an older model.

It has made collecting data easy, and I can compare my progress as I work to become a better runner.

Battery life is acceptable, I'm charging every 5 days while using GPS 30-45 minutes a day.

The Garmin Connect App works well. Link it to myfitnesspal and you have a fairly complete fitness tracking app.

Garmin also links with mapmyrun, Nike+, and Endomondo to name a few.

This watch also works with an Garmin hear rate monitor. (010-10997-00).

There are many great running watch choices available, so you will want to do your research.

Of course you can always just use you smart phone and any of several great free running apps.
A lot of those have voice feedback so you don't need to look at your phone.

title: Good Basic Case
review_text:
This is a good basic case that takes a little getting used to.

Nothing fancy here, but it works well. The case holds the kindle securely. The kindle is secured in place on all four sides with one side held by a Velcro flap tucked underneath the kindle. I can't say that the kindle will never fall out, but as long as the stitching holds up, the kindle is not going anywhere. The case is thin and comfortable in use, but provides no protection if you drop it.

You have access to every thing while the case is closed. Magnets keep the case closed and serve as the auto on/off function.

The case does not slip in your hands, but there is no hand strap here.

You can fold the cover back and tuck it in a flap for free standing horizontal viewing. You get one position. This feature seems flimsy when you look at it, but I have not had any problems. It feels secure in use.

At start up and shut down of the kindle it seems like the case was designed upside down. This must have been done so that the camera is on the top when the free standing position is used. This puts the on/off switch at the bottom when the cover is held like a book.

It took me a few times to get used to this, but now it's automatic. Once you are up and running the auto rotate feature takes over.

The only other issue I have is as the case comes up to the edge of the screen in most places, I have problems pulling down the main menu at times. This could be because I'm a new user, or I lack coordination. To solve my problem, I rotate the unit so that the camera is up. The camera has a big window, so I can always pull the menu down from that area.

Bottom line, if the stitching holds up over time this was a great choice. If it doesn't, it won't be the first time I wasted ten bucks

Upgrading review

Pros:
The braided cable is a big plus for preventing flexing. The rubber collar at the connectors should prevent premature breakage. Frequently loses contact in the middle of large image file transfers

Snowkids (vendor) immediately responded to my concerns and shipped me replacements. 5 stars for customer service and standing behind product. Second cables are a bit tighter.. Would give a 4.5 if possible

title: Sirui K-40x Ball Head Outstanding Quality/Value for Rock Solid results
review_text:
I was looking to purchase a gimbel head for a Nikon D750/Nikkor 200-500mm lens that was rock solid with my older heavy duty Bogen 3011 legs. A salesperson at Pro-Photo in Portland guided me over to this and I was wowed at first sight. Sitting next to the $400 ball heads I could immediately see the quality and value at about 30% of the cost. That translates to me as part of another lens or a few B&W filters. I have also recently paired a Fuji S5Pro body and Sigma 50-100mm Art lens. Both of these combos are just too heavy to get tack sharp shots handheld... and my attempts with a heavy mono-pod have been ok.. but less than perfect. This is not a tripod head/leg combo I envision carrying on my next vacation or on a hike through the mountains... I am 60 and have been buying and using tripods since I was 15. I believe in the heaviest tripod I can carry when I'm shooting photos out at 300-500mm and further. When I pop a spotting scope on and try and track targets out at 300-400-500 yards, a solid, pin point image saves a whole lot of walking. There is always a little creep with that last twist to maximum tightness...but once you get the hang of the tension wheel... I have yet to see my focus point move even slightly when locked in on an eagle nest for 10 days. As with other reviews I find the panning a little stiff... but if I was filming and airshow or Indy Race I'd probably put on a fluid video head instead. I anticipate many years of service and it will still be working long after I am. Today I ordered a Sirui K-30 from Amazon because while the K-20 is probable adequate for a D300 and D7100 with smaller lenses... who knows what I will come to own in the future... That's the one I'll carry to Hawaii with the light carbon-fiber legs. There is a great review on DPREVIews called Battle of the Titans.. Excellent quality with the bonus of an outstanding price point. I also have a lightweight Sirui carbon mono-pod that travels in my suitcase. 5 stars because the pros overwhelm the small cons.. I can live with those

George B Sitka, Alaska

title: Hardware does not work - don't wast your money.
review_text:
The original dac+ board comes with (4) standoffs, (4) screws that go into one end of the standoff, (4) nuts that go on the other end of the stand offs - all work fine. Notice (4). This kit comes with (2) standoffs that are too short (one with no threads), (2) standoffs that are too long, (2) short round head screws, (2) short flat machine screws, (2) long screws ~1+ inches. The boards, boxes all have (4) holes or threaded sites. I could find no way that worked (including using the original standoffs from the DAC+ kit) with this set of parts. There were no directions, but that is not the even the main issue. Any configuration of parts for this kit should have (4) of what ever is needed to connect the items together.

Pic shows the hardware that was sent. Returning for refund.

*** suggestion to the manufacturer: there is a much simpler way to do this. Look at your step 1. Put (4) standoffs in vs 2 and make them long enough so the Dac+ board does not bend. Now PI board is anchored to the base. Then put the DAC+ board on the (4) standoffs. Screw ((4) standoffs through the DAC+ board holes into the standoffs that you just put in. Now you have both boards secured and 4 open screw holes in the top standoffs to secure the case top with (4) short screws. Simple and likely you could have all standoffs the same.

title: Beautiful matte screen is so easy to see
review_text:
We have a high end Sony 55" in the living room and a sub three hundred buck off brand tv in the guest room and the difference between the two is instantly noticeable - image quality and sound are in two different lanes entirely. This Samsung Frame is in the master bedroom and I am in love.

The matte screen means almost no reflective glare at night with lights on in the bedroom. That's something I did not realize bothered me about our other two tvs until there was no more glare. No matter where I look at the screen, it's clear and I don't see the reflection of my bedside lamp.

This tv does weigh more than the other two we own in the same size. I would definitely not try to move this or wall mount it alone. The box has a complete wall mount ready to install, but I don't want this that high since it's a bedroom television, so we installed the feet and set it on a table. This also comes with an old school box for connections rather than just plugging everything in directly to the television. That's a little old school, but it makes sense because they intended for the tv to be used on the wall as an art display as well and you don't want visible cables hanging off that.

As far as the art viewing goes, that's really nice if you are willing to pay for the subscription. I am not, but viewing the samples is pretty cool. This is a Google and Alexa friendly voice control set up and I do like that. The free Samsung TV app is very nice - it's sort of like Pluto TV, but proprietary to this television brand. Lots of free channels and a ton of choices at no cost. We use Netflix, Prime, HBOMax, and Paramount Plus as our paid streaming options - no cable or satellite here, just streaming. Everything works seamlessly and smoothly. My favorite thing here though, is so simple and small and I can't understand why every tv doesn't have this - the remote control is SOLAR powered!! No more buying batteries and it works well.

title: Comfortable, easy to customize
review_text:
My old smart watch was much loved, but after two years, it stopped charging all together and I needed a new one. This one is a smidge bigger over all, but easier to see. I primarily use it for tracking steps, tracking sleep and the time at a glance.

The sleep monitor is pretty accurate and let you see how much REM sleep vs light you're getting each night as long as you're wearing the watch of course. The corresponding app on my phone shows the week or month info as well. The pedometer seems to be lagging a bit when compared to another one we have - one of them is off.

I have not set this watch up to do text messages, call notifications or to control music from it - you can do that, I just don't need all that when my phone is already in my pocket. However, connecting this watch to the app via my Samsung Note 10 was easy and relatively painless. I do love that I was able to customize the display so show a photo of my dog on the face and just the time & date. I don't need the other info all crammed into one screen. You can easily scroll through the watch menu for any data you need. So far, it's survived daily wear out in the desert, in my office, at home with the dogs and out riding horses.

title: Gorgeous picture, full rich sound, easy to set up
review_text:
After almost 3 weeks with this television, I am amazed and very, very happy with it. There's a lot to like here and a couple of things that I wasn't expecting from any television.

First is the ease of set up. Our previous smart tv was a ROKU and reasonably simple to set up as well. The Google connection here means just signing in with your existing Google info and the tv uploads your existing apps. Just like moving to your new Android phone or tablet. All of our streaming apps populated and we were able to sign in without drama - HBOMAX, Prime, Paramount Plus, HULU and Netflix. We only stream and haven't used cable or satellite in 5 years, so easy app access with a new tv is important.

The 4K picture is outstanding. There's no distortion in picture quality or digital noise even from old 1940s movies. The colors are rich and full and the tv settings let you adjust to your preference as well. We've watched a lot, A LOT of tv recently and every show on all platforms has been gorgeous. Frankly, we probably watch way too much tv as a rule and that's not going to change. I've been amazed at the picture quality difference between our year old HD tv and this one.

We've connected Alexa to this tv and the voice controls work...most of the time. Using the voice control via the remote control renders better responses for sure. The tv has recognized a Fire stick, Roku Express stick, and a portable DVD player for us without any drama. We don't have a gaming system, though.... I'm considering buying one for this giant screen.

But my final show stopper moment with this television has been the sound quality. We've never had a tv that didn't require a sound bar. Until now. Despite the tv being quite thin and lightweight, the speakers still produce a deep sound quality without any tinny undertones. The settings have a calibration option for the speakers that you definitely need to do for the best sound - it works. I truly believe this is the best television we've ever owned.

title: Gorgeous, astonishing battery life. Crisp, clean sound for music and books
review_text:
I have a pair of the Masters & Dynamic Leica edition and I absolutely love them even after almost a year. Lately though, my husband has been skulking about wearing them so trying these out was a no brainer. I've used these MW50s for three weeks now and I actually like them better.

First, the rich saddle color leather is really beautiful and there's no mistaking these headphones for some random pair. Second, they connected via Bluetooth to my LG V40 phone, my old Sony Xperia phone and two different Samsung tablets easily and quickly. Third is the excellent battery life on these. I've literally listened to music and my Audible audiobooks for three hours at a time for four days in row before recharging them. That includes getting a couple of calls. No cauliflower ear and the heat build up is slower.

I listen to a little of everything - country, classical, old rock etc. I can clearly discern the French horns in classical music as well as the background banjo in some old country music. I don't know about the quality of heavy bass with these simply because I don't listen to heavy bass music. Audiobooks with full production recordings, are clear and crisp - I can detect background sound effects comfortably without any fuzziness or distortion. Bottom line is these are worth that eye opening price if you use them every day and appreciate style as well as function.

title: UPDATE REDUCED TO 2 STARS Beautiful sound, amazing with the 500 as a group.
review_text:
UPDATED REVIEW REDUCED TO TWO STARS JUNE 2019

We've had trouble with the remote for three months now. It works sporadically at best and has finally died entirely. This is a major problem because you cannot do important stuff with the sound bar without the original remote control. Such as.... rebooting it. If you change your WiFi network like.... getting a new router, then you cannot simply go to the app and update the connection. You must reboot the entire sound bar via the remote control only. WHICH DOES NOT WORK AT ALL. This design flaw has rendered the entire sound bar none functional because it cannot connect to the new Wi-Fi - going back to our old router isn't an option because it died. So now I have a sound bar that technically is operational, yet cannot be used. Our Bose 500 sound bar was able to be reconfigured for the Wi-Fi swap because it's remote works like a champ - it's also significantly simpler in design than the 700 remote. (I'll end up spending fifty bucks for a new 700 remote and that really aggravates me)

******* Original review before the drama*******

We've had an older Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System in our living room for a couple of years and we've been pretty happy overall. I recently put the Bose 500 version of this sound bar in our master bedroom and was amazed at the difference, so getting this 700 for the living room was a no brainer. I mostly just expected them to connect as a group and have the same sound, but this 700 is better than the 500.

It's a long, narrow, sleek looking unit with glass finishes that makes it almost invisible in front of the Tv. Our Roku fits alongside without drama. The connections are via digital optical cable or the HDMI. Just turn off your TV speakers - not mute, off from the tv settings. You need to use the included wired headset to fully set the speakers for your room's accoustics. I'm using this bar with a 55", 3 years old, Sceptre dumb tv and a Room streaming stick - the connection was immediate and drama free.

You must use the Bose app to get full functionality out of the sound bar. The app let's you connect two or more Bose speakers with the tech and use them all simultaneously as a group to play music or audiobooks etc. The app also starts the set up for the Alexa link and the streaming services like Prime, Tune In, Bluetooth streaming and others. You can also set 6 favorites as one touch launch options.

Alexa works fine through the sound bar, but the response speed is noticably slower than through a regular Echo. I get a glitchy message saying "This unit is unable to perform routines" every time I say "Good morning". Good morning triggers a specific set of actions from Alexa to turn on our bedside lamps, the bathroom lights, turn off our porch lights, give me the weather and then our daily news brief. Despite that glitchy message, every morning, the Bose performs our routine flawlessly. It's weird, but not a big deal really.

The sound quality is excellent and immersive in multiple settings from music to a movie. The app let's you adjust the sound quality and balance with bass, treble and center. You can also set it for dialogue mode to enhance/clarify voices and reduce background noise - this is very handy for the news or a talk show. Take some time to adjust the settings for what your ear really likes and you'll be amazed at the fullness of sound and all the background details.

After two weeks, I'm incredibly pleased with the build quality, looks, sound and full functionality of both the 500 and 700 units. The 700 wins out by a nose over the 500 for us because the sound is bigger, but mostly because the remote control is better. The remote lights up when you lift it and you can find the buttons instantly. I programmed our TV to the Bose remote and it controls the sound bar, channels up and down and power for both the tv and the sound bar. Bottom line is that I am now looking at buying another 700 for the master bedroom and moving the 500 to our guest suite so we'll have the full set.

title: Beautiful music, crisp television, immersive movies. Some Alexa functions missing
review_text:
There's a lot to love here with the Bose 500. We have a Denon Soundbase w/ Bluetooth Streaming Audio in our master bedroom and a Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System in the living room - both are from 2015. I'm replacing the Denon unit with this Bose 500 for several reasons, but primarily for significantly better sound quality and Alexa integration.

This is connected to a 2014 Samsung smart TV via the HDMI port. I had no issues connecting the sound bar to the Bose Music app (be sure you get the correct app from Google Play). Next you find the sound bar with the Alexa app and link your Alexa account to this machine. All I had to do for tv sound was turn off the TV speakers through the tv settings and press the tv image button on the Bose remote. Be sure to have 2 AAA batteries on hand because they don't include them for the remote.

You plug in the included headband and use the app to fully calibrate the best sound in your room by sitting in five different locations and letting the headband and sound bar talk. This takes about 6 minutes and it's definitely a step worth doing. The sound from this Bose is amazing - playing Beethoven or Hand Zimmer's soundtrack from Hannibal is immersive and gorgeous. The television is equally good - you can use the app to set the tv sound to dialogue centric for a talk show or regular for movies. You can also adjust the settings for the sound to increase/decrease bass and treble and to move more to the center or sides of the projection speakers. Once you get it set up exactly to your preferences, it can feel like a movie theater without the volume blasting you away. I'm especially loving rewatching Firefly with the Bose 500. The app also let's you do 6 preset favorite music streaming stations from Tune In, Amazon, Spotify and another service.

As to the Alexa functionality... This is actually pretty good with two glaring faults. The sound bar is always listening for the wake word like the Echos do and there's a privacy button as well. I have noticed a tiny lag on a few requests, but it's not constant. I've been getting a weird message telling me that this unit is not compatible with my Alexa routines, then it performs the routine perfectly. (For example, I say good morning and Alexa turns on our bathroom lights, the bedside lamps and gives me the weather) It's a bizarre glitch, but as long as the routines are completed, I don't care.

The first real problem is this unit cannot link to your other Echo units in a music everywhere group - I'm not sure if that's a Bose issue or an Amazon proprietary issue because our Harmon Kardon Alexa speaker cannot be linked either. This is a shame, but not a deal breaker for me, but it's still an issue. The thing that does aggravate me is that this unit is unable to connect to and read my Audible audio books. I get a message that says it is not compatible with Audible at this time. The work around is simply to use Bluetooth and stream my book via my phone or tablet. That's ridiculous with Alexa integrated into the sound bar. This may not bother anyone else, but I listen to audiobooks more than I read now and having that full body, room filling crisp audio is a great thing.

Bottom line for us is that we love this sound bar for television viewing and music. It's sleek and modern and just does it's job. In some ways, the Alexa integration isn't complete, but the basics are there for most functions. It's definitely an improvement over the old Denon box we used to have and it's even better than the Bose Solo 15 in our living room.

title: Better for watching wildlife than the heavens. Easy assembly and use
review_text:
I've never owned an actual telescope before, but my father had a couple of them and we used them often. One was really high end and fancy and the other was more like this one - a beginner's, casual scope with limited abilities.

We had this one unpacked and put together, ready to use in about 20 minutes total. The instructions are a little lax, but they do cover what you need to do. There are three different lenses with it and they are relatively easy to swap. The tripod is sturdier than I expected actually and it's quite stable on the cement patio and driveway.

However, I was a bit disappointed with the difficulty of trying to track and focus on a specific night object. Where we've really enjoyed using this telescope is at the farm in daylight. It's a lot of fun watching the horses and deer at distance just doing their thing - my friend even spotted a fox strolling by our pond yesterday at dusk. For my family, this is better suited for wildlife observation that night sky exploration.

title: Features only with expensive monthly membership. Camera images are high quality, works with Alexa
review_text:
This is one of those products where I really like the gadget itself, but absolutely hate the company and policies behind it. Enough so that I would never actually do business with or trust the Canary company with my personal financial information.

The camera itself is sleek and easy to use and set up. It connected via Bluetooth and wifi in minutes and upgraded its own software immediately. You have to have the app going first to get the camera online and running. There are blue, yellow, white and red lights on the bottom that sort of tell you what the status is - it's actually a pretty solid copy cat of the way the Alexa Echo devices do things.

I've been impressed with the clarity and detail in the camera both live streaming and the short recordings. The night vision is remarkably good - that alone warrants a five star review if the policies didn't ruin everything else. Setting up the app and camera to determine Home, Away and Night modes is ok, but doesn't always work. Right now Canary is alerting me that a person has been detected - IT IS ME! I set it to home mode, but the camera just doesn't believe it. I was able to connect the Canary with Alexa in the Alexa App Skills and watch live streaming of our living room on the bedroom television via the Firestick - completely painless.

Here's my problem. The so called three month free trial of the Canary membership requires a full credit card input BEFORE you can use the free trial. Umm.....no. I don't know this company, there's zero information in the app about exactly how they secure our info and if after the trial is over, you want to cancel, there aren't clear directions and a single step CANCEL button. It's about as sketchy as can be. All the features you might buy this camera for are locked unless you pony up that membership fee. Honestly, I'm just sick to death of being nickled and dined every month. This camera should include a SD card slot and it doesn't. Bottom line is that I have no idea if the microphone works or the downloading of recordings because the free trial isn't actually available unless I give them credit card access - never going to happen.

title: Fine craftsmanship, high quality materials. Really good sound quality and comfortable
review_text:
I'm not an audiophile by any means, but I do appreciate excellent quality recreation of certain types of music and full cast production audiobooks. I don't like earbuds for more than a few minutes at a time for a number of reasons so I try to always have a good set of wireless headphones around. My older Sonys are very good, but beginning to show their age after three years of regular, reasonably hard use. I think these will serve nicely as replacements.

The form factor here is just as nice as the actual function and that's not always the case with high dollar electronics. The materials are very nice and put together flawlessly - the entire unit is really gorgeous. These are actually quite heavy in the hand, yet balanced so perfectly that I don't notice the weight at all wearing them. The ear pieces are attached with magnets to the arch piece of you can remove them for cleaning or swaps in the future. The lambskin is very soft and doesn't cause excess heat build up for my ears.

Pairings with my Sony Xperia phone, my Samsung tablet and a Fire tablet were all easy and painless. I've used these headphones for streaming music via Amazon, Pandora and my own stuff from my cloud files plus Audible books for a couple of weeks now. I'm currently using them on vacation right now with the included travel case - they fold up a bit and the charging cable & 3mm direct connect cable fit in the case as well. Sound quality is excellent as well here for my types of music - primarily classical, country, and 80s pop. I can clearly hear the French horns, flute, or soft cellos in Hans Zimmer compositions or a Beethoven concerto. Aretha Franklin sounds great with these BTW. (I can't speak to thumping bass reproduction because I detest that style and don't listen to it.)

title: Hefty, very loud volume, beautiful sound quality. Does not link to Echo, Dot or Fire TV
review_text:
As an avid fan of Alexa, I am delighted to have this Harman Kardon Alexa speaker. I've had my original Echo since the first week they released the initial invitation to buy and have since added a Dot and Alexa controlled thermostats, dining room lights, Fire TV sticks and plugs through out the house. This unit was meant to enhance the music sound quality from Alexa and expand our Alexa listening group and work with the living room television.

The speaker itself is considerably larger than my original Echo - wider and heavier. The lights on this are brighter as well - when playing music at night or listening to a book, you can leave the light on and it works as a night light. You can also turn the light off if you prefer. Setting this up takes a bit longer than my Echo or Dot - it's slower making the initial WiFi connection, but once you link to Amazon via the Alexa App, you're good to go. It connects via Bluetooth to both my LG V10 phone and my Samsung tablets without drama.

This unit is significantly louder at every volume setting than the original Echo and makes the Dot sound like she's whispering. I have this in our formal living room where we have 30 feet tall ceilings, grass cloth covered walls and an enormous open space - the room was designed for correct accoustics with my Grandmother's grand piano and music simply sounds beautiful in here. The Harman Kardon Alexa sits on a table where the piano used to be and the sound at volume 4 simply envelopes you no matter where you are in the room. Set the volume to 6 and I can hear my book or music two rooms away almost as if it's floating through the halls. The sound quality is excellent and playing Beethoven or opera or country music renders each instrument precisely from tiny flutes to cellos and twangy fiddles. I'm immensely pleased at the improvement from the Echo to this for just music.

The reason for the one star deduction is because I thought/expected the Harman Kardon to by fully, 100% integrated with Alexa. It is not. This unit cannot be linked to the Fire TV sticks, meaning that I cannot use it to verbally control the living room television. It cannot be linked to my Echo and Dot units. That means we can't include the Harman Kardon speaker in our multi room group so the same song/book can be heard throughout the house. We cannot do the Drop In skill where Alexa acts as an intercom system for multiple rooms. There are a couple of other skills this speaker isn't able to perform simply because it doesn't speak to the Amazon Alexa products. If they can correct this glaring deficiency, then this would be a five star product and one i would consider buying for the guest suite and master bedroom. As a stand alone Alexa unit, this is a top notch choice, but if you want to link to your existing Echo, you can't do so.
