title: Great Media Device...Terrible Tablet
review_text:
Okay, there are three types of devices which are this size. One is an ebook reader. If that's all you want, get a Paperwhite. Seriously, try reading on the Fire's screen for half an hour and it will be like reading on a computer screen (not so good for the eyes). Especially in low light!

The second is a tablet, if that's what you want then get a Galaxy Tab. I have a Toshiba Thrive, which is similar to the Tab (one step down in some respects, the same in others) and that blows this out of the water in terms of what it can do and how it does it. But it isn't the best at playing back movies. eBook capabilities are similar and screen is similar, so if you aren't going to watch movies on it then DO NOT BUY A FIRE HD!!!

The third type of device I call a portable media device. And here is where the Kindle Fire really shines. The screen is currently the best screen available on a 7" device. And the sound is great. Using the built in application, I can play movies ripped from DVDs with great sound and video. On my Thrive I have trouble with this, getting jittery video and low sound most of the time and no consistency. A free program will convert your videos over to Kindle Fire screen size and save them in a format that the Fire can open (search for them, there are many and lots of free options so don't pay for that).

The negatives are, however, many. The Kindle Fire HD sports the UGLIEST user interface I have ever seen. Some replacements are available, and I'm debating them just like I am debating rooting the device to get the Play store. Note that if you have an Android phone, without rooting you can not get your paid apps on the Fire. Also, you can access only a few thousand of the half a million apps that other Android devices offer. This is just because Amazon wants to reduce piracy by restricting apps that may get around protections, but it costs hundreds of thousands of legitimate apps. Also, Google apps are not present (except gmail), so you can't get Google Maps or Voice or the like without sideloading or rooting. I'm not sure why Amazon hates Google, since Google gave them the framework for this tablet! I got the $25 screen protector and I don't like the feel, but that isn't the tablet's fault.

If you have kids, Amazon's kidtime app is great. Other similar apps are available for other devices, and if you want any content this one costs $2.99/month for a one child license, but it is a good app and they did a great job of integrating it so there are no bugs which could cause your kid to find their way out accidentally (or on purpose for those smarter kids out there). If the service was free for Prime members, or if a limited version was free for Prime members, I would rate this app as 5 stars and perhaps raise the entire Kindle Fire HD up a star since that would add one great use which I currently am not taking advantage of.

Oh, and there is no SD slot, no USB slot for external drives, and no IR port so it can't be a remote control (all very disappointing).

Having said all of that, I am keeping mine for movie playback and occasional reading when on a plane or in a doctor's office. I have a 10" tablet which I love and wouldn't trade in for this Kindle if they paid me. But since I can have both (thanks mostly to putting several people together to buy me one present together), this is worth keeping.

title: Not Bad For Beginner Users, But Most Of Us Can Do This Anyway
review_text:
Pros: If you are a beginner to computer networking and you just want to host a cloud server at home for tablet and smartphone access to your music and video library, this is the device for you. Set-up is simple, anyone who can install a Linksys router can do it, and tech support is decent (for the purposes of this review, I called and asked them to help me with a non-existent issue so I could report that they do in fact help people, then I told the guy I was a mystery shopper and thanked him for his help).

Cons: If you have Carbonite back-up service, if you have a WD MyBookLive NAS, or if you know how to configure any of the several dozen software packages that do this for you, then you can already do this for free without buying this device. Yes, I do mean that there are free packages (at least for Android phones) which you can download and use to make your computer into this device without any fees whatsoever. So for anyone who is mid-level or above in computers, this is not a worthwhile purchase.

title: A Good Idea Poorly Implemented
review_text:
Let me start by saying that if you happen to be looking for a way to record music from one of the 41,000 radio stations that this company supports and then take it to your car without having to record it yourself and put it on an mp3 player, it does work.

That being said, the stations are not very inclusive. This isn't going to be XM radio we're talking about. most of the stations are non-US stations (which is a good thing for some people, but not what I was looking for). I wanted children's music for my kids to listen to. I love XM's Kids Place Live, and I wanted something like that. What I found was less than a dozen channels, only 4 in English, and at the time that I set this up all 4 were playing music that wasn't appropriate for my kids. So I decided to move on to pop and use it for myself. This was even harder. There were about 100 top 40 channels, mostly not in English again, and the ones that were were just random stations like 94.9 FM in Nashville, TN (I couldn't tell anything from the names and there is no way to get user reviews of the stations). So I picked one at random and decided to record it just to write the review and then I can add this to the pile of gadgets that I don't use anymore.

That wasn't easy either. You have to start it recording, let it go for the amount of time that you want (this isn't mp3 downloading where you can get a few hours in a few minutes), and make sure your computer doesn't go to sleep. Also, the station dropped out after about 20 minutes and when I came back 4 hours later I discovered that the software doesn't reconnect you automatically, so you really have to use this to listen to music at your computer and then replay the same music in the same order in your car.

The device is also missing features that I just assumed it would have like identifying when songs start and stop to separate tracks, identifying the music and labeling the tracks so I know what I am listening to, or the ability to mark a song at the unit while I am playing it back and later be reminded to go buy that song.

The device was very easy to set up, despite the fact that my 64 bit version of Windows doesn't support their 64 bit client and I had to run the 32 bit version (not a big deal just not sure why they bothered to include the 64 bit version if it doesn't work). I updated to the latest software quite easily as well.

This is a buyer beware situation. The device works as advertised, but has no bells and whistles that aren't mentioned in the product description (like auto-reconnect, which I would consider a standard part of this device's operation). And it is easy to use (if you don't mind baby sitting it). But you can access 100 times that many radio channels online and record them using free software that will do these other things and then download them to your mp3 player in minutes (assuming that you have one, if not check out the Samsung ones and remember to get one with speakers if you will ever want that capability, don't waste your money on a Zune or an IPod unless you have a good reason to).

For me, the product was a free test product, so I didn't waste anything. but I would be returning this if I had paid for it.

title: Perfect Headset, Perfect Operation
review_text:
EDIT: My original review is below, but here is some extra information: After two months of use, this device is still working well, but the silver paint is almost all gone and the case I bought for it is not rigid so the button keeps getting pressed in and the battery drains every day. I need to find a better way to carry it... The paint problem shows a definate lack of quality and if I could change my rating I would reduce this to a 3 star review.

I have had this headset for two days now, so this reviewer can't speak of the potential for battery problems or how durable it is. However, so far I am very impressed. The quality is beyond compare, I have carried on several conversations and then said "by the way, I am trying out my new headset, how does it sound?" and the response it always that they didn't know I was using one! I am so happy to have found this because I get nervous driving and dialing, plus I tend to drive fast and I like to have both hands on the wheel. I'll be buying the car kit next, but I still want a headset for use while walking around and while at events or fairs.

I have a Motorola V600 and it paired easily, though since this was my first bluetooth device and there is a pairing code to enter I had to read the quick start directions. From the time I opened the manuel to my first call it took 3 minutes.

Cons: It didn't come charged, which I get upset about because I am too impatient to wait. Also, when you plug it in it can take up to 5 minutes before registering the plug, which made me think that it was broken at first. Next, it doesn't come with a belt case and it is a strange size so buy the belt case (I am waiting for that to come so look for my review of it later on). And finally, the battery is not removable (I found out that this is typical of these headsets, but I still would have liked to be able to buy several and change them out).

Other than that, it is a perfect headset. Since those are minor problems and are typical of other headsets, I rated this model 5 stars.

As for me, this is my first bluetooth headset. But I know people who have problems with other headsets and this one outperforms all others that I have seen...

title: Great value for the amateur and semi-professional
review_text:
So you are looking for a good lens? You want something that will take great pictures, but you don't want to spend hundreds or thousands of dollars? Well this is the lens for you! I have used several 70-200, 70-255 and 70-300 mm lenses in stores which considering them and the answer is simple: You can't beat a Nikkor lens.

This lens has excellent clarity and optics. I am the director of the Nicholas Copernicus Observatory at the University of Miami and I have extensive expierence in optics. I can tell you, without a doubt, that you wont find a better lens than this for twice the price. I have only bought Nikon cameras and lenses, but I get plenty of chances to use other ones at the observatory as different people bring their equipment to learn how to use it better. No matter how many cameras I use, I still recommend Nikon above all else.

I presently use this lens with a Nikon D70s camera.

There is a more expensive version available, the Nikon 70-300mm f/4-5.6D AF Nikkor SLR Camera Lens, which has superior optics. I highly recomend that lens if you are a professional who needs perfect clarity on sunny days for nature photography at the 300mm length. If you are an amateur or even a semi-professional, if you use this in lower light, or if you are using the shorter length most of the time, save the $200 price difference and save it toward another lens!

title: Great system for your office or living room
review_text:
I needed a small system for my office. I wanted removable speakers, good sound at all volumes and a sleek look. This system filled that void. I searched for about a month to get it, and there is nothing less than fantastic about this system, even the price.

In terms of sound, I can understand music at all volume levels (many cheaper systems distort at low levels) and at high volumes it sounds great. I can't use it at high volumes now that I've taken it to work, but I am thinking about buying another for my living room at home (run the output of my family room stereo and I'll have a system that sounds good in both places for parties).

In terms of looks, this system is very cool. I tried to downplay it by placing it behind my desk, on the shelf where I keep my food, so that people wouldn't question it (because small stereos are allowed but not everyone likes us having them). Despite my attempts to blend it in, I've received several complements on the way that it looks. Silver casing and a sleek design are just the basics, this system features a blue backlit display that looks great!

I thought that the "DVD" option in the stereo meant that you could play MP3s on DVD (a great idea for someone who wants to never have to change CDs), but in fact it meant that the system is a DVD player, and it has a video output to connect to your tv. That's a nice plus. I haven't tried the MP3 idea yet, so it may or may not support them.

The stock antenna is terrible, but so are most stereo antennas. I'll buy a new one soon... The other downside is that you can't switch between presets without the remote (you can change the station, but not using presets). But with 30 FM presets, I'll never run out! The only thing that wasn't obvious about the set-up is that the disk buttons (disk 1, disk 2, etc) on the stereo are the eject buttons, not the select buttons like most other stereos. Overall, this is a great design for a great stereo. I used to work at a radio station as the engineer and now I wish I had this back then because I could blast music in my office and really utilize the system the way it was meant to...

title: A bit of Advice
review_text:
The other reviews and the description seem to properly describe this camera. I am writing this review to give you the perspective of someone who started out with film SLR cameras in school, then got a digital 5MP camera and have used that for years and am now finally getting into Digital SLR photography. This is a big step back into the professional circle for me, and I'm anxious to get out to the zoo or to some vacation spot in the mountains to do my professional photography once again. I purchased this camera almost a month ago and my opinion is that it is the best camera ever made under $2,000. This camera has everything you can need.

I want to warn you, get the full set with the lense. This lense sells for almost $400 and is about the best all around lense you can find. Don't go for the cheap models. I wrote a list about this camera that may appear on this page for you to look at, but be sure that you get the ML-L3 wireless remote (for $20, how can you go wrong) and a spare battery (2,000 pictures sounds like a lot, and I haven't needed to recharge in this month that I've had the camera, but remember that when you go on a trip you may forget to recharge and you don't want to get stuck). Also, get a tripod (try the Slik Tripods U9000, I wrote a review of it and I find it to be the best buy around for a light-weight tripod that acts like a much heavier one) and get a carrying case (the jury is still out, I haven't found one that I like, I want one that will hold two cameras, 4 lenses, a large flash and a bunch of accessories).

If you aren't sure if the D70s is worth the money over the D50 or the D70, it is. The improved autofocusing system is much better than the others and the larger LCD is worth all the tea in China! I leave the LCD protector that came with it on and have no problem seeing my pictures, even outside. Although this is a larger camera than the D50, it isn't much of a difference and you will regret going with the cheaper camera.

If your budget was lower, save up and buy this camera. I bought a CoolPix 5000 a few years back and always kicked myself for not going with the D100. Now I've gone with the best camera on the market and I'm perfectly happy. Plus, I have the satisfaction of knowing that none of my friends can show me a better camera (unless they spent $4,000 or more on a D2X or D2H, and none of my friends can afford to do that)!!!

title: Good product but takes some getting used to
review_text:
I got my Kindle Fire HD for Christmas and ordered this case because I wanted a keyboard and the price seemed right. There are some annoyances that I listed under Cons, but to me they're not dealbreakers. I am happy with this case and really like having a keyboard with the Kindle.

Pros:
The case securely holds the Kindle. I definitely feel better about letting my kids play games on the Kindle while it's in this case than when it's not protected.

I like the look of the case overall. The stitching is sturdy and the leather is nice. It's like a little dayplanner when it's folded up. (I kinda wish it came in a solid color though. All black or all white or all red would look better to me than highlighting the closure in a second color, but that's just my personal opinion.)

I love how light the keyboard is and how it can "clip" on and off magnetically.

It was super easy to set up even though the directions were written like they were translated into English from a foreign language.

I thought the little red flap at the base would get in the way of typing but it really doesn't. It can fold underneath or just be held down with my wrists without any discomfort.

Cons:
I am not sure how to tell when the keyboard needs to be charged other than to plug it in whenever I remember. A red light appears while it's charging then goes away, so I assume it's ready at that point. I haven't used it enough for it to wear out completely, but I wish there was a way to tell how much charge it has left since I use the keyboard here and there and don't want to charge it all the time, especially if it doesn't need it. (But I also don't want it running out on me.)

The keyboard is small and I haven't gotten used to it yet. One example is that the apostraphe is made by hitting Fn+L, and I keep forgetting that then hitting all kinds of wrong buttons trying to backspace and fix it. This is frustrating because I can type 108 wpm on a standard sized QWERTY keyboard without many mistakes. I think this will just take some getting used to due to its small buttons/size. The keyboard is in great shape though, and I haven't had any sticking or falling off keys like some other reviewers have mentioned.

The Kindle seems to take a while to recognize the keyboard each time. It gets a little annoying when I just wanted to type something quickly and be done. (I am still unclear if I am supposed to go into my Wireless/Bluetooth settings each time I turn on the keyboard or if it will in fact recognize the keyboard eventually if I just wait. I usually lose patience and open up the settings.)

In order to charge the Kindle, I have to either take it out all the way or lay the case flat and open the bottom velcro flap. So it can't really be used with the keyboard while it's charging.

The case doesn't really work vertically. If you fold it in half, the keyboard gets in the way and needs to be removed. And it doesn't stand up vertically on its own.

title: A portable hub that's a perfect companion for my Surface Go 3
review_text:
Recently, I was looking for a tablet that is functional and portable. I settled on the Surface Go 3 for its capabilities to function as a laptop while being as portable as an iPad. I've been satisfied with my purchase and as with the purchase of any new device, a set of cases and accessories are necessary.

One such accessory is the iVANKY 7 in 1 USB C Docking Station. This neat little hub has everything I need for my new tablet. It has a microSD and SD card reader built in, which means that while on travel, I can use it to offload pictures from my mirrorless camera into my tablet to do some simple editing and to posting when I'm back at my hotel and the 3 USB-A ports allows me to have an extra copy of my photos on an external drive.

Back at home, I can use my tablet as a full desktop with the help of this hub. I have my keyboard and mouse receiver connected to the USB and an external monitor connected via the HDMI port. The video quality is great and the audio goes through the HDMI as well.

Now we can talk about the Type-C PD passthrough. The type-c PD port on this dock can take up to 100W of power and pass it through to the tablet, meaning that while I'm at home, a single USB-C connection takes care of my charging, video, audio, and keyboard/mouse. This product earns its name of a docking station.

This dock is great for travel and at home. It's simple and straightforward.

title: Audio drivers are hard to find, lack of support, and computer freezes randomly.
review_text:
I've purchased quite a few compact computers previously and all of them have little quirks that I have to deal with but in the end, I'm able to set them up with the necessary drivers and use them without issues. This Kamrui CK 10, though...

On paper, the specs of this computer is impressive. A 10th generation i7 processor with the integrated Intel graphics which I already knew wouldn't be winning any awards in the gaming department but that's expected. With 16 GB of ram and 512GB of nvme storage, this computer is a good starting point for anyone who needs a fairly powerful PC in a compact package.

Regarding the ram: I've disassembled this computer and found that the ram is soldered to the motherboard, as is the CPU. This means there is no way to upgrade the ram.

Regarding the storage: There is good news here. There are two M.2 slots supporting NVME so SSD storage is quite expandable. I installed another 512gb ssd in the secondary slot.

The operating system that was included was a vanilla Windows 11 Pro with absolutely no additional bloatware aside from what Microsoft has already included. This is good. All drivers were installed and the machine booted fine.

So in my case, it is customary for me to install Windows from scratch when I buy a new computer. It's just something I do. I don't trust that there are no hidden software in the preinstalled systems. As such, I needed to locate the necessary drivers for this computer.

As expected, Windows will successfully detect the graphics, wifi and bluetooth hardware. Also as expected, the Intel chipset drivers needed to be installed manually. All standard so far. With all of this done, there were three pieces of hardware that were unidentifiable. These were the sound drivers.

Scouring the search engines, I couldn't find the drivers for the CK 10. I finally located Kamrui's facebook page, which led to a linktree that then led me to their forums. In the forums, I searched and found a set of drivers for the CK 10. Unfortunately, that seems to be for the CK 10 with an i5 cpu. It did not contain the correct drivers for the sound card.

I resorted to searching for the drivers by device id. From there, I pieced together the necessary drivers to get sound working. I had to use drivers from three different driver sets from HP.

I did reach out to Kamrui's support email. They responded two days later but rather than read what I wrote, they responded with a canned form for me to list my product, serial, purchase date, etc.

So what else is wrong? Well, at least twice per day, this computer freezes without warning. It could be caused by the sound drivers that I had to piece together but how would I know? I don't can't actually get the right drivers for it.

title: Displaylink sets this dock apart.
review_text:
[[VIDEOID:8052bc9e6eb256b6a38698f645a9fee]] So you purchase a laptop or compact PC with one or more USB Type-C ports maybe not knowing much about the technology. In truth, the Type-C port is a huge mess. There are so many functions that the port is designed for that a normal consumer would have a hard time understanding all of them. In my case, the type-c port on my computer doesn't support HDMI video output. This port came in handy with its Displaylink technology.

As a dock, the iVANKY 15 in 1 Triple Display dock is a great product that, if your laptop has USB charging capabilities, can connect all of your external devices with just one USB plug. You can connect multiple external monitors, external USB drive, your keyboard/mouse, and gain the ability to read SD and MicroSD cards, all with a single plug. In terms of charging, the PD port outputs 18W of power which is good enough for fast charging your tablet and phone, and the computer port outputs 94w, powerful enough for many laptops running a CPU up to an Intel i5. All this is packaged in a modern, metal shell and it even has a 100w power adapter included.

Already, this is a great dock, but the DisplayLink feature sets this dock apart from the rest of the pack. DisplayLink allows a computer to output video to a computer monitor (up to 4K) through a standard USB 3.1 port. This means that if you have a type-c that doesn't support video output or if it only has Type-A ports, this dock can still give you the ability to add more monitors to your setup. Just install the included drivers (the dock shows up as a computer drive when you plug it in) and this dock will extend your desktop.

While it is a little pricey, this dock has the quality and functionality to justify it.

title: A solid enclosure with RGB goodness

When I first got this M.2 NVMe and SATA SSD Enclosure, I was concerned about its build quality. The enclosure opens by squeezing the plastic at the top and sliding the drive mount out like a drawer. I felt that the plastic felt soft and didn't understand why it's not metal.

Oh, and the enclosure comes with both type-c to type-c as well as type-c to type-A connectors cables. Other enclosures just come with a c-to-a cable.

title: Sometimes, just a simple hub will do.
review_text:
[[VIDEOID:676a9c562ee284b4873a8774f1caf9d6]] With modern computers cutting down on the number of ports, relying on the speed of USB 3.1 Type-c to handle all of the I/O load, consumers now have to provide their own docks or dongles. This means that we are dealing with more cables and what is termed "dongle hell". This is just the reality, unfortunately. It's both more convenient (a single cable to connect all of your accessories) and less convenient at the same time.

Well, this isn't the fault of the HENRETY USB C Hub, it's just here to help resolve the problem that you are facing... and it does a good job of it. The hub is sleek, with an aluminum shell and high-quality ports.

In my use, I already have a small dongle to connect my laptop to an external monitor but I ran out of ports for it. I needed more ports, but I didn't need another HDMI output. I opted to save some money and get a simple USB hub and it really does work very well. I have a backup external drive connected that I periodically backup my video editing projects to and I also have my Dualsense (PS5) controller connected to it. I haven't had a problem yet.

If you just need some ports without the fancy HDMI, ethernet, and audio outputs save some money and get the Henrety hub.

I have a few M.2 solid state drives in external enclosures for various purposes in my computer tool kit. I have one that I use to store files that come in handy while installing Windows. For the NEMIX RAM Nemisis Series 1TB SSD M.2 2280 PCIe drive, my purpose for it is to use it as a backup drive for my video and photo editing projects. title: Good features and powered by mains.
review_text:
While solar-powered cameras are convenient, I've found that they have too many compromises when it comes to functionality. In order to save on battery power, the software usually shuts down the camera when there is no activity. Usually, that means nothing gets recorded until the motion detector is set off. In addition, a couple of my solar cameras actually had firmware updates that made them almost unusable because the app can no longer wake the cameras up. When transferring data, this cable will allow you to copy files at the highest USB 3.1 speeds.

But more than that, this cable supports video signals so that it will be usable to connect your laptop or phone to a portable type-c monitor (assuming your devices support it).

Personally, I got this cable to work with a pair of NReal Air video glasses so that I have a backup to the cable included in the box. These cables work but are a little bit stiff.

title: Great concept.  A compact surge protector with a lot of options
review_text:
The TROND Flat Plug Power Strip Surge Protector is a great concept. Everything about it shows that some thought has been given to its design. Unfortunately, their choice of materials weren't as well thought out.

Some design concepts that attracted me to this surge protector is that it gives you 8 power plugs in a surface area that's just under 4 x 4 inches. The four plugs at the top are grounded while the 4 on the side are two-prongs. In addition, the wall plug is flat, giving you a lot of options as to where you can plug this product in. Finally, there are three USB-A ports and one USB-C port.

However, as I've mentioned, some design choices are questionable. As with many surge protectors, the USB ports are under-powered. The Type-A ports are not too bad at 5V/2.4A, but there is no quick charge capability. The Type-C is not PD, so your charging options are no better than the Type-A ports. You're stuck with 5V/3A with a total wattage shared between them at 14W or 3.4A.

My second gripe is with the build material. Compared to many power strips, the plastic covering this product feels quite cheap. It has a smooth texture and just feels... thin to the touch. The same plastic also covers the wall plug. In addition, the power wire is thinner than other power strips that you'll find. They feel more like the two-prong extension cords, except that it has three wires.

Now, I don't have proof that their choice of materials will be an issue at all, but it does give me pause.

title: Could be a little taller and more firm.
review_text:
I converted a small room in my house into a useful room where the floor is covered in Japanese Tatami mats. These mats are used for everything. Sitting, lounging, and sleeping. It's a different concept from Western style rooms where the furniture is based around sitting on a sofa or chair. In a tatami room, everything is lower by a couple of feet.

In the room, we have floor chairs that are great for lounging on but what makes it even better is the ability to do some work in that room. This laptop desk was just the thing. With a tilting top surface, foldable legs for easy stowing, book and cell phone holders and even a small drawer, this desk seemed to be everything we wanted.

I do have to say that it really is something that I love using, but because of how often I need it, the shortcomings jump out at me every time. Firstly, the tilting function is fairly useless because it can only tilt at predetermined angles and nowhere in between. The tilt is just too much because of how low the table is. Tilt the table and it is touching your lap.

The second problem is as I said, the height. If this was a couple of inches higher, it would be perfect. As is, my lap barely fits under it.

The last problem is that the table is wobbly from side to side. It's just not very stable. I can't put a cup on it. I'm forced to use a either a closed bottle or a shelf on the side.

While this will work for now, I'll be keeping an eye out for a better table if one exists.

title: Multi device support with built-in mousepad.
review_text:
So how do 3's add up to a 4? If you want to talk about the typing experience for the HAMOPY Portable Tri-Folding Wireless Keyboard, it's a 3. When considering the track pad experience with this keyboard, it's also a 3. However, I'm giving this product a 4 overall because of what it can do, despite the experience being less than ideal.

Firstly, this keyboard/touchpad combo has quiet keys that are smaller than the keys on a laptop so your hands would have to squeeze in a little and if you have big hands, you're not gonna have a good time. Because of the folds, the keys are also somewhat compromised. The keys along the folds are squashed, especially the V key. With that said, between typing on a tablet screen or this keyboard, I'd choose the keyboard any day.

The touchpad can also feel a little bit cramped and somewhat insensitive when it comes to dragging, which is a tap and hold to start a drag. It does have the standard two-finger tap for right click and two-finger drag for scrolling (the scrolling direction is opposite of what I'm used to). While this touchpad will not be preferable over a tablet's touchscreen, it does work very well on machines that do not have a touch screen, namely a FireTV stick.

That is where this product shines. The two scenarios I listed were Typing with a tablet and typing/mouse with a FireTV. This product can do both with the press of a button. Able to be paired to three devices at once, I have a single, portable keyboard/touchpad that works with my three most-used devices. The trifold design makes this thing easy to pack into luggage or to simply stow away at the coffee table and easy to bring out when performing a search on the FireTV.

Great product whose versatility makes it worthwhile.

I use an HDMI KVM to control multiple computers. This KVM has an optical output which extracts the audio channel from the HDMI port. I use this optical connection to connect to the 1Mii bluetooth transmitter.

The 1Mii Bluetooth 5.2 Transmitter for TV to 2 Wireless Headphones is a transmitter with an optical and a 3.5mm headphone jack inputs. On the output side, this device transmits through bluetooth 5.2 and supports various bluetooth audio standards such as APTX. You can connect up to 2 bluetooth devices to this transmitter and both will be able to hear the audio.

I picked up this transmitter to replace another transmitter because the 1mii has volume controls that is missing from the other transmitter and dedicated buttons to pair headset 1 and 2. After the replacement, I found that the audio coming from the 1mii was not as loud as my old transmitter. This is a glaring problem that you will face every day when using this device.

To clarify this a little bit. I pair this device with an open ear bone conduction headset so that I can hear my surroundings while having the computer audio also in my ears. I can certainly put in an earplug to get better sound, it would defeat the purpose of using the open ear design when working at my computer.

title: Saved my headset
review_text:
These SOULWIT Cooling-Gel Ear Pads Cushions were not made for my headset, which is a USB gaming headset by [[ASIN: B01E8RS598 Sades]], which is no longer being sold.

Ear cups are pretty much the first thing to go on a headset and unless you have an expensive brand, it is hard to find a replacement cup for your specific headset. After two years of use, the cup of my gaming headset was falling apart and leaving little bits of plastic on my face after I use it. Rather than throwing away the headset, I wanted to try and find something that might work with it. I got lucky with this SOULWIT ear cup. It is attached via a stretchable flap, which is exactly how my old cups attached to the headset.

As you can see from my pictures, the shapes of the cups weren't the same as the originals had an odd angle to them but in the end, they fit and they are really comfortable.

The material is glossy on the sides, but where it touches your head, it is a soft cloth. I don't sweat a lot when I wear these so sweat being absorbed into the cup isn't an issue here, but I can see where someone who sweats will have problems with it. The gel is soft and comfortable.

I really love the new cups and the fact that I'll get more years of use out of my headset.

title: As advertised
review_text:
USB Type-C is just a super complicated situation all around. The ports themselves can be USB 2.0, 3.0, 3.1, 3.2, thunderbolt 3 or thunderbolt 4. I'm probably missing something there. That only covers data transfer speeds. For power, a Type-C port can be rated for multiple voltages and amperages. To protect the consumer from disaster (or they try anyway), each type-c product needs to be equipped with a chip that allows it to negotiate the speed and voltages. This includes the cables. The situation with cables is just as complicated. A cable may only be able to charge at 5v and not carry any data. They may carry only usb 2.0 data. Better ones may be rated for high speed data but not high wattage. Others have both high speeds and are rated for up to 100w. Good luck trying to find the right cable once all of them are dumped in a drawer somewhere.

This 240W USB C to USB C Cable 6.6ft is yet another odd one in the bunch. It is rated for high charging speeds but is only USB 2.0 for data. Why is it necessary though? I have a Dell Inspiron laptop that has a discreet NVidia RTX 3050 processor. This means that it has a high power demand.

This Dell was also designed to charge only from a USB type-c port and the input power must be 130w. So began my search for a charger that I can take with me when I'm away from my desk. I was able to find a macbook style charger that outputs 140w but I didn't own any cables that were rated for higher than 100w.

I came across this cable and connected everything up. During boot, the Dell's firmware still detected a low-powered charging device, but when I booted into Windows 11 and checked its power settings (after reconnecting the charger to the wall), Windows did not warn of an under powered charger as it normally would. I was then able to use this charging setup to play a graphics intensive game for over an hour with no sign of GPU or CPU throttling.

In the end, this cable allows me to have a portable solution for my laptop without having to lug around a standard laptop charger. It works.

title: This did come with any plug converters because you shouldn't use them with this product.
review_text:
Traveling with electronics is inevitable and when traveling abroad, it's necessary to understand a few things about the places you will be traveling to. Language, currency, electrical standards, and cell phone bands being a few of them. Traveling to the UK or Europe, 220v is the electrical standards. To deal with this, you must understand the electronics that you will be bringing with you. Most modern electronics such as cell phone and laptop chargers will work fine at 220v with a plug adapter (make sure you check the power adapter regarding input voltage), but personal electric devices such as hair dryers and maybe electric shavers might not. There are two choices here. Look for hair dryers that have a switch to allow 220v or 110v. Otherwise, purchase a voltage converter.

The BESTEK 2000W Travel Voltage Converter power strip is one of the more powerful voltage converters that I've seen. Most voltage converters will not support hair dryers because they don't output enough amps for the devices to work. At 2000W, this voltage converter power strip is powerful enough to power most dryers out there (many work at 1800w). This device is well labeled to reduce any confusion. There are two output sockets. One rated at 200w for less intensive devices such as the electric toothbrush and my camera's battery charger. The other socket outputs the full 2000w. This is good for the hair dryer.

I was disappointed that this device doesn't work in the UK and since their standards are a little different from the EU, I didn't want to even try using a plug converter to try it. There's no guarantee as to what wattage the plug converter can handle so it's better to play it safe. Use this device only in the European countries and the others that are listed on this web page.

For me, I didn't take any chances with it. Since the USB ports are fairly standard at 2.4a output but no quick charge or type-c PD, I charged my phones using a different, more robust phone charger. I used this power strip only for the hair dryer with nothing else plugged in. Even then, I don't know that this thing can handle running the thing for too long.

In the end, I think the better strategy is to purchase devices that are rated for both 110v and 220v to save yourself some headache. I was able to find a third-party oral-b electric toothbrush charger rated for 220v and a travel hair dryer with the 220v switch. I'll still have this power strip with me for my camera until I can find a third-party charger for it.

title: Great for a beginner like me!
review_text:
I've been watching a bunch of electronics repair videos lately and thinking back at my past purchases and the electronics I threw away, I wondered how many devices I could have rescued. Determined not to let electronics repair scare me off from tacking them, I decided to start collecting the tools that I need to do my own repairs.

I started with an affordable, but well-reviewed soldering iron: the Pinecil. A good silicone mat (same one as StezStix Fix), and now a microscope.

The LLIMINK Digital Microscope 7'' LCD, Coin Microscope is a great product. In the box, you'll find all of the accessories you'll need to get started, including any cables that you might need. What I wasn't expecting of this device is that it is actually battery powered and that the battery is removeable (see my pictures) -- very much in line with the Right-To-Repair philosophy. The remote control was a nice addition as well (taking a picture seems to be only controllable from the remote so make sure you don't lose track of it).

The base of the microscope is aluminum with two built-in LED lamps that are separately powered from the microscope itself. They provide additional lighting from other directions if you need it. The microscope itself has bright leds that shine directly downward on the board.

If the microscope mounted LEDs are causing too much glare, there is a collar that can be fitted to the scope. It will block the LEDs and instead, reflect them so that the light is indirect. Kinda like the lamps the dentists use. You're not blinded by the bulb when you're looking up at those lights.

Moving on to the screen, it is a 7" screen with passable quality. The viewable angle isn't great but it gets the job done. Any issues with the screen quality is solved by connecting the included micro-hdmi cable to your monitor. I've included pictures of both the 7" screen and the ouptut from my monitor.

I've already done a couple of simple projects with the help of this device. I built a garage door opener and gate opener using microcontrollers that are connected to my home automation system. I'm building my confidence with electronics and soldering. Hopefully, I can keep more devices out of landfills by repairing them myself.

title: Good for IOT or guest WIFI networks, but wouldn't reconnect to my main router after a reboot.
review_text:
The Wavlink N300 Wi-Fi Range Extender is a quick and easy way to extend your 2.4gHz network to reach the remote corners of your house. It is easy to set up if you're familiar with normal router setup procedures (connect to its wifi or via ethernet cable, then access the router configuration through a browser). It will normally create a wifi SSID that's different from your original wifi, but you can just force it to use the same name.

For my phones and computers, I use my 5G wifi network but the older 2.4 Ghz is great for home automation products such as switches, doorbells, and cameras. Keeping those devices separate from your main network will keep your main network running smoothly and free up a lot of IP addresses on that network.

This device is very stable once it is set up. My IOT devices have been able to communicate at a good speed and have not lost connections yet.

Unfortunately, this extender did not automatically connect with my main router again when I rebooted it. In fact, I was forced to reset the device and set it up all over again in order for it to work. I can't say for sure that the problem is caused by this device or by my main router. It's just my personal experience. Perhaps test this functionality while you're still in your return period for the product.

title: Sleek and powerful with Type-C charging
review_text:
The Dell Inspiron 14 Plus 7420 Laptop, what a sleek little machine. It has a nice slate grey color with a matte finish. It is thin, it is powerful, and it just fits what my wife uses it for, which is some office work (word, excel, emails) and some media consumption (videos, social media, etc). Pretty much what everyone would need a laptop for.

Unfortunately, I'm unable to test this computer to its fullest with some games or video editing because I haven't been able to pry it away from my wife since she got it.

Looking simply at the specs of this machine, it is obvious that the i7 12th generation with the Intel Iris integrated graphics will be able to handle anything a casual user would be able to throw at it. The 16gb of ram will handle a LOT of browser windows and application being open at the same time. The 1tb ssd is actually great to have considering that many laptops only include half of this storage. Lastly, the 2.2K resolution is perfect for this small 14" screen. It's higher than full-hd 1080p and isn't too high to where the text and icons are barely legible.

The keyboard is the standard chiclet keys with good travel. It is quite and works well enough to not cause typos or missed key presses.

The screen is comfortable to look at and at 14" it allows this laptop to be a great portable workhorse.

Overall, I'm impressed with the stability, comfort, and just the build quality of this product. With the powerful CPU, I expect that this machine can last for quite a few years.

title: Good as an outdoor screen but not sure this is better than a painted wall when used indoors.
review_text:
Just as my title says, this 100 Inch Front and Rear Projector Screen is an acceptable projection screen for backyard movie nights but not great for indoor use.

It is a large piece of white, stretchy cloth that can be tricky to set up. Without a frame, you would need to figure out a way to stretch the screen taut without it sagging too much in the middle and you need to have these hooks set up well in advance of your event because it can take some time. Once you have a good setup for it, the screen is easy to hook up and stow away. It will fold nicely without leaving any creases the next time you need it again.

When used indoors, you will find that this screen leaks a lot of light through to the back wall because it is made to also be a rear projection screen and because of that you're probably losing a lot of the light that should be reflecting back to you. That's why I say that I don't think it works any better than a painted wall when used indoors.

The price of this screen is pretty low but just be sure you know what you're getting into with this screen or you'll just be disappointed.

title: Beefy, portable power that works with my Pinecil soldering iron
review_text:
This portable power bank is quite beefy and has some real heft. It weighs 2.5 pounds without the case but with this heft, you get some real power.

It sports two Type-A ports at 18w max, a type-c port at 45W max, and a 110V AC output at 120W max. The type-a ports are fairly standard and isn't anything out of the ordinary. The AC output should be enough to power most laptops but you would still need your laptop's power adapter.

The type-c port was why I wanted this device. It can be used to charge this power pack at 45w, which means you can fully charge this thing fairly quickly (sorry, I haven't timed it). The 45w output of the port allows me to run my pinecil soldering iron at full wattage, which means that my soldering iron can go to 300 degrees within 10 seconds.

Another use I had for this thing was that I had a skunk that was breaking into the crawl space under my house and I needed a camera to keep an eye on the movements of the skunk. Rather than purchasing a motion sensing camera, I was able to take one of my WIFI cameras and power it with this thing. The battery not only lasted the entire night, it only went down by one light (out of 4 lights total).

Two things I wish this power supply had: An adjustable DC output with a barrel connector. This would allow charging of laptops without having to plug in the laptop's adapter. I would also have liked the type-c port to support 100w because many laptops that charge by Type-C require at least 60w output. Those laptops will trickle charge from this power bank but will complain about it being under-powered.

title: Perfect for my Dell XPS 17 gaming laptop with RTX 3050
review_text:
Docking station or second power adapter? That's the question one would normally ask when considering a travel solution for their laptop. A docking station that sits on your desk with all of your accessories and monitor plugged in is a great solution that leaves the OEM power adapter available to be left in your travel bag. In the case of my Dell XPS 17, a docking station really isn't available for an affordable price.

The XPS 17 charges via the USB type-c port just like most laptops out there today, but it requires a 130 watt input through that type-c port. Most type-c docks or even power adapters only go up to 100w. If you wish to force the issue, the Dell thunderbolt dock will cost you over $200.

This 130w power adapter was the best solution for me. It truly delivers 130w as Windows does not give a warning regarding a low-powered power source when it is plugged in.

I had an extensive test of this device a few weeks back where I used it for three days straight. Initially, I thought it felt a little hot to the touch, but after rebooting my laptop, that no longer happened. I believe it was a problem with Windows power management.

This adapter comes with a nice, braided cable on the USB type-c side (normal two-pronged power cable on the other). The cable isn't overly stiff and feels like it has good build quality.

There really isn't much else that needed to be said about this adapter. It outputs the power as advertised and it worked great when I needed it. This will be the adapter I take with me on travel and my other adapter stays at my desk. Love it.

title: Fun little device
review_text:
The Frameo Digital Photo Frame 10.1 inch WiFi Digital Picture Frame is a fun little device that looks great on my family's piano. The matte black frame, while being plastic, doesn't look cheap and looks great on the satin-black finish of the piano.

This Frameo frame is basically a 10 inch android tablet without the built-in battery that tablets include. The OS is locked down by Frameo's customizations so only the frame's functionality is exposed. It would actually be nice if it can also display a webpage at the click of a button (to display weather or the dashboard for my home automation system) since it should have the capabilities to do that. The screen is 1280x800, which may seem low, but in practice, the pictures look clean and the backlight is really bright. I didn't feel like I was missing those extra pixels that higher resolution frames may have. That was pleasant surprise.

Setup for this device is quite simple. Set up the Wifi, download the app, and you're ready to send pictures from your phone to the picture frame. It's really great that you can share your pictures on this 10.1 in screen easily and quickly. Go out on a hike and took some great pictures? They can immediately go into the picture frame's slideshow rotation when you get home.

There is no account to sign up so anyone can download the app and input the sharing code generated by the frame to start sending pictures -- even over the Internet (which may or may not be a draw for you, depending on how security conscious you are).

With the ability to send over the Internet, I am planning on purchasing a second frame to gift to my parents. My brother and I can then send pictures of the kids to the frame every once in a while and my parents can have a nice frame to see their grandkids that is constantly updated.

title: This is a powerful vacuum/blower that works well for all sorts of functions
review_text:
The Xasla 15000mAh Electric Air Duster & Vacuum 2 in 1 is a great little device that works great for cleaning more than just a computer.

I wanted this thing for its blower functionality because it is always a good idea to clean out the vents in your computers once in a while to make sure they don't overheat. I have a laptop cooler that I use for my gaming laptop and that thing does get visibly clogged up with dust after about two months. It is great to have this thing around that I can just pick up and clean it whenever I want.

Obviously, this is intended as a replacement for canned air. Canned air can get into very narrow areas because they are equipped with a narrow straw to concentrate the airflow. Also because of how narrow the straw is, the air is very strong. The Xasla is not as powerful and the nozzle isn't as narrow as an air can's straw so it is not able to get into those deeper areas, but for the advantage of not having to worry about air running out in the middle of a cleaning and the convenience of having it available at all times, I think this is worth it.

The vacuum functionality is quite good as well. The first time I used this device as a desktop vaccum, I found that the suction was quite weak. Then I looked more closely at the device and found that there's a switch to change between blower and vacuum mode. After making the switch, the vacuum function worked much better. The difference between the two modes is that when the air exhaust is directed to the blower nozzle, there isn't a good amount of air flow to make a good vacuum. Moving the switch redirects the exhaust to a side vent that allows much greater flow.

This brings me to the only complaint about this device. The side vents was blowing on the desk while I was trying to vacuum up my desk. This is somewhat counter-productive, but in the end, it still got the job done.

One last thing about the Xasla 15000mAh Electric Air Duster & Vacuum 2 in 1. The battery handle is detachable and can be used as a battery pack for your phone. This is a nice bonus feature that can come in handy as well.

title: Some issues, but suits my needs
review_text:
[[VIDEOID:385afc8b9bb77a3a87ae44bd958be49a]] This double din aftermarket car radio has some great features, most important of which are the wireless Android Auto, wireless Carplay, and steering wheel controls. On paper it all sounds great, and it's really affordable to boot.

The implementation of the whole thing is just a little bit janky, but we'll get to that.

Installation:
I purchased a wiring harness for my Toyota Sienna 2009. My car is not the XL with surround speakers or dvd player so the wiring is really simple. Surprising to me was that the wiring harness colors matched up to the colors of this radio's wires exactly. Just match the colors and connect them together.

For steering wheel controls, it is necessary to patch into three additional wires: sw1, sw2, and sw gnd, which I located by searching google for "2009 Steering Wheel wiring diagram". I found a diagram of the back of my factory radio and using that, found the pins that the three wires ended in.

This radio didn't fit the generic mounting bracket for my van. It was almost as if the screw holes for this radio was drilled upside-down. If I were to mount the radio upside down, all of the holes would have lined up, but right-side up, they don't. Fortunately, the mounting bracket is plastic so I was able to drill the holes that I needed in order to successfully mount the radio.

Operating System:
This radio runs a rudimentary operating system with basic radio functions. It also seems to have the ability to play music from a USB drive.

The configuration options are limited. I found that I am unable to adjust the backlight of the radio at all and the screen is actually quite dim.

Android Auto:
Pairing of Android Auto is very easy. Simply connect the phone to the radio via a usb cable and choose the android auto function. Follow any on-screen prompts and you are connected. Disconnect the cable and the radio will try to connect to the phone wirelessly (make sure wireless AA is enabled on your phone).

The performance of AA can be a little laggy when compared to my other car, but it works well enough to bring my old car into the modern age.

Honestly, I'm actually okay with most of these issues because it is still much better than the original factory radio that lacked bluetooth and GPS. Being able to connect my phone to use its smart functions is all I really wanted out of this radio and that's what it delivers. Plus, I can still use my steering wheel controls. I'm satisfied with this purchase

title: The best low-priced led projector I've tried thus far.
review_text:
[[VIDEOID:6e49ad5f11d43ea1130e7014d1f00ce9]] I've always been interested in video projectors because I really wanted that theater experience at home. Previously, they have been out of reach because of the price of the devices as well as the price of the bulbs that required replacement.

title: Survived the wash, but I wouldn't suggest that you try it yourself!
review_text:
These Omidyi True Wireless Sleep Earbuds are my second pair because I accidentally threw my previous pair in the wash. Surprisingly, my original pair survived and this pair is now my backup.

Here is my original review:
These earbuds aren't bad at all, if you use earbuds to fall asleep. The advantages these earbuds have over wired ones are, of course, the wires. I used to go through wired sleep earbuds fairly quickly because I tend to pull on them quite a bit when I sleep. There are no wires to tangle here.

What makes these earbuds "sleep" earbuds are that they are much smaller than normal wireless earbuds (see my picture). They sit flush in my ears and don't protrude. In general, depending on your ears, these may actually allow you to lay sideways and still be comfortable. In my case, I can lay against my right ear without it hurting me but I can't do the same with the left. I often end up using only the right bud.

In terms of sound quality, due to their size, these earbuds will not be loud nor will they have great sound depth. The battery life also lasts about 5 hours due to their size.

I still really like these buds because I do like them more than wired ones but I don't use them any other time.

title: Good, basic machine with a discreet graphics card and plenty of ports
review_text:
This HP Pavilion desktop is a solid, but basic PC that, while it can be considered a gaming PC with its discreet Radeon RX 5500 card, that isn't going to raise too many eyebrows with its specs. What's out of the realm of this machine would be 4K gaming and VR, but it can run most modern games at medium settings at 1080p.

That's not why I needed this machine, though. As a Plex server, this serves well. It is quiet and can transcode videos using hardware transcoding. Unfortunately, it only has a single slot for an additional hdd. As a video editing machine, it can handle 1080p videos, but will struggle with 4K. As a photo editing machine, it can edit pretty much anything from the devices you have, but if you work in print, you'll find this machine lacking. For emulation, this machine will work quite well for all classic systems and even some more modern ones. Of course, for everyday web browsing and watching videos, this thing will be more than enough.

Overall, this is a fairly priced machine that is a step up from the basic computers that one may find and the discreet GPU will help to make this machine last longer than those with embedded graphics.

title: Good headphones that leave your ears open so you're not cut off from the world.
review_text:
Bone conduction headphones have become quite popular and because of this, there are many to choose from. This specific model is quite minimalist. A thin metal frame with the vibration units and electronics hanging off it.

In terms of comfort, there is no adjustability to the metal frame so it may take some getting used to because the frame may feel like they are too big or too small depending on your head size. For me it felt a little bit loose but I came to realize that it actually stayed where you place it and it really wasn't a problem.

For sound quality, this bone conduction headphone will never match a nice pair of over-ear headphones but that really isn't what it's for. By leaving the ears open, one is still able to stay aware of the surroundings, making it great for cycling and jogging where hearing the traffic is essential for safety reasons.

A pair of earplugs are included with this product and with one or both in, one can really appreciate the difference between regular headphones and bone conduction. You can still hear the music (or in my case, audiobook) through the earplugs because of the bone vibration but all outside sound is cut off. This means that you'd be able to listen to music over the sound of a loud machine.

I have tried a few different pairs of bone conduction headphones and these are the ones that I have stuck with so far. The buttons maybe be somewhat limited (just two buttons that control volume and power), but they are easily reachable and not hard to press and the IPX6 means it's water resistant against rain and sweat.

title: Great mobile router with a T-Mobile restriction
review_text:
I love GL.iNet. They create routers based on OpenWRT, which has so many great features that you'd find in professional level routers that cost thousands of dollars. There is a fairly steep learning curve to it, though. Fortunately, GL.iNet understands this and makes things easier by creating their own customizations to the firmware to make OpenWRT easier to use and more custom to the routers themselves.

The GL.iNet GL-E750 (MUDI) is their latest 4G LTE router. Pop in a sim card and the router will create a hotspot that routes to the LTE network. For additional protection, it is easy to set up the router to connect to a VPN provider. By connecting the router to VPN, all client computers connecting to it WIFI will be protected.

I used this router during my last trip and it was GREAT. I have a few devices that I bring with me. A laptop, tablet, and phone. I even bring a firetv with me sometimes. While in the car, I have the router connecting everyone's devices to the Internet via LTE and when I got to the hotel, I connected the router to the hotel's wifi and turned on VPN. The transition from LTE to hotel wifi was seamless. Not only did I not need to reconfigure everyone's devices to connect to the hotel WIFI, we were also secure behind the router's firewall and VPN connection.

The two restrictions that this product may present to potential buyers is first, the price. It is quite pricey and it can be hard to justify its purchase. Especially when you can get a travel router for around $40 with the ability to tether a phone via USB. The second issue is that this specific router is tied down to the T-Mobile network with no ability to unlock it for other networks (according to the seller's response in the questions section of for this product). If the convenience and the ability to fully control the TTL to bypass t-mobile's tethering throttling restrictions is important to you, it may justify the price you'd be paying.

title: Runs on old variant of Openwrt firmware.  Hope they address it soon.
review_text:
I love GL.iNet. All of their routers can run on either their own openwrt with added custom UI and ease-of-use packages or you can install their provided barebones openwrt. You can even download and install the firmware directly from Openwrt.org if available.

With that said, the GL-AX1800(Flint) WiFi 6 Router is a disappointing product. In the last year, Openwrt has made setting up a mesh network of routers using 802.11r and 802.11s but only if you're running version 19.07 or higher. I wanted this router in the hopes that I can upgrade to WIFI 6 for my custom mesh network but I was sad to find that the variant of the firmware is based off version 15.

While gl.iNet has backported all of the necessary security patches from the newer kernels, it won't help the many power users who have come to depend on the new Openwrt version.

Due to this, I didn't give this a thorough test to figure out its stability and wifi speed as both of these can be affected when/if the company finally updates the firmware to a more recent version. Meanwhile, this router will sit in my closet waiting for its day to shine.

title: Good if you want to use these for swimming, I guess.
review_text:
These bone conduction headphones are waterproof (IP68) and come with 16GB of storage so that they would work while swimming (bluetooth will not work well under water and really doesn't have the distance to cover a pool). They can be fairly loud and can be heard even with (especially with) earplugs.

The advantages of an open-ear, bone conduction headphone is that you can hear everything going on around you while still being able to listen to your music or audiobook. Put earplugs in your ear and you can retreat into a more private listening experience.

The disadvantage is that the sound quality is just not going to be as good as headphones that cover your ears. That is especially true for this pair of headphones.

The sound quality from these headphones is not good. The lows are barely audible most of the time and when you turn up the volume to try and hear more of the lower tones (including human voices), the higher tones are already too loud. This is alleviated by putting in earplugs. The plugs will block most of the higher tones as those come out of the speakers themselves while the low tones come in through the vibrations.

Another issue I have is that the buttons are horrible. They are made of a single piece of rubber on the outside and the buttons themselves are recessed pretty far in. title: A basic projector with great brightness and full HD resolution
review_text:
The WEWATCH Video Projector with WiFi and Bluetooth is a basic projector that has all of the necessary features that one needs.

The description of this product may lead you to think otherwise, but this projector is not really a "smart" projector. It does not run on Android and the built-in user interface is quite basic. Yes, it will play videos and show photos from USB drives and it has WIFI... for whatever reason (I didn't really look into it because I simply plugged in a FireTV). The bluetooth, on the other hand, does have a function. I'll get into that in a bit.

So for video input, you have two full sized HDMI ports, a VGA (for those ancient laptops that your office may have lying around?) and a USB port which outputs enough amperage to run a fireTV, so no additional power adapter necessary.

There is no automatic keystone adjustment, but what is there works well. You can adjust the four corners up and down, although I found that it still seems to have some bloating in the middle no matter how I adjust it (could be a problem with my projection screen and projector positioning). A tip for doing the adjustment: If you aren't able to move the corners in the direction that you need, try adjusting the zoom first. By zooming out, it allows the corners to be pulled up or down more.

Audio is as expected in that it is not winning any awards. It can get pretty loud, but it still sounds empty. This is where bluetooth or the 3.5 mm headphone jack comes in. For wireless audio, you can either pair a bluetooth speaker/soundbar to the projector itself or you can pair the speakers directly to the FireTV or whatever dongle you're using. The advantage of pairing the speakers to the projector is that they will work for both HDMI inputs. If you really wanted to get full surround, you'll have to extract the audio out of the HDMI wire. Basically plug the HDMI into an audio receiver, then the audio receiver to the projector. The receiver can take care of decoding the surround depending on your setup.

For the brightness, the 1100LM beats out many other projectors of this price and resolution. You can really tell that the picture just pops. It will work well enough in a dimly lit room, but you can only truly appreciate it when the lights are completely off.

Overall, this is a low-priced projector that will work well for outdoor, temporary use, or even a permanent setup inside the home.

title: All-Metal.  That's good and bad...
review_text:
I listen to audiobooks to fall asleep at night so I wear "sleep" earbuds as to not disturb my wife. I usually buy the soft silicone type, which never have good audio quality, but does the job. They usually break withing a couple of months because I tend to tug on them a lot when I sleep so this time, I decided to try out these ceramic Wired Headphones with Microphone.

My initial impressions of these earbuds are that they have better sound quality than the other sleep earbuds that I've tried. They also have excellent build quality. There are silicone reinforcements at all of the wire connection points to protect them from failing due to tugging and the shape of the earbuds are as flat as possible.

When in my ears, these metal earbuds do not protrude at all, they lie flat. I tested by lying on my side to see if they would hurt but they seemed okay because nothing protrudes. Then after a couple of nights, I found that while direct downward pressure doesn't hurt, the earbuds do hurt when they are nudged from side to side, which happens when I'm shifting positions at night.

So overall, I'm still using these earbuds and have gotten used to them, but they do still hurt occasionally, depending on how much I move at night.

title: No keystone, 720p native, bright.
review_text:
The Salange 7500 LUX Mini Home Projector is a barebones projector that provides good brightness, good focus, full-sized HDMI input, but not much else. Connect a FireTV or AndroidTV device to this projector and you have all of the "smart" features that you'll need.

So the good of this projector is that it is somewhat compact, not as small as the pico projectors, but small enough... it's about the size of a bread box (as the saying goes). The focus ring is fairly tight, meaning that once you find your focus, it won't move. The USB outputs enough amps to power a FireTV and overall, it is very straightforward to use.

The bad is that there is no keystone adjustment, not even the analogue kind that tilts the lens. The resolution is only 720p and I found that projecting at a shorter range of around 9 feet, I'm able to see every pixel on the projected image. At a longer distance, the pixels may meld together better.

In summary, this is a low-priced projector that will project an image through an HDMI input. If that's all you're looking for, this will work, but if you're looking for something that you may set up more permanently, this isn't it.

title: Acceptable for portable storage, will probably not cut it for PS5.
review_text:
The Centon Premium SSD at 1TB is priced higher than even the WD_Black while claiming faster speeds. Before I get into my conclusions, I need to say that I'm only testing this drive through a USB enclosure so the conditions aren't optimal, but my conclusion about this drive is in comparison to another drive that I test through the same enclosure, meaning all conditions are the same between the three drives.

I had two other drives that I was able to performance test against this Centon drive. The first is a [[ASIN:B09575SWX5 Pioneer NVMe]] drive at 256GB and the second is a [[ASIN:‎B08695D3VW Klevv NVMe]] drive at 512GB. All three drives were placed inside a USB drive enclosure and connected via a Type-C cable capable of video transfer (meaning it's made for data transfer, not just charging).

Because I'm only testing through USB 3.1, I'm not expecting to reach advertised speeds but using the relative performance between the three drives under the same conditions, I can make some conclusions. The Pioneer drive is advertised at speeds of up to 2,100/1,600 MB/s and in my setup, I was able to reach 1,041/937 MB/s which is quite impressive. On to the Klevv drive: it is advertised at speeds of up to 2,050/1,650 MB/s and my results for this drive was 915/922 MB/s. title: easy to use, nice clamshell design, but a little bit too flexible.
review_text:
The Samsers Wireless Portable Folding Keyboard is only 1/2" thick when folded, and of course, half that when undfolded. It is quite thin and portable. It caught my attention because it supports pairing with up to 3 bluetooth devices simultaneously and with many of us having multiple devices (phone and tablet is quite normal), these devices are great for someone like me.

The clamshell design means that the keys are protected when closed. It also holds itself closed magnetically, and powers on my simply opening it. Pairing is easy: hold the function key and press one of the Q,W, or E keys to select one of the three bluetooth slots, then press the big "connection" button on the left bezel of the keyboard. This all seems pretty slick to me but I did have one concern with this keyboard's design and that is the hinge system. When the keyboard is open, it is quite easy to twist it with just a little bit of pressure. It means that I'm always extra careful when I'm taking it out of my bag.

In terms of functionality, the keys are a the same size as the ones on my laptop and has the same amount of travel as well, although they are a little bit louder than my laptop's keys when typing. I'm using this keyboard to type this review right now. What I found is that the keys are a little bit unresponsive. I keep missing letters every few words I type. Just in this last sentence, I had to go back about 5 times to correct missing letters. This defeats the purpose of purchasing a keyboard to type more quickly on a mobile device. Perhaps if you are normally heavy-handed when you type on a keyboard, you wouldn't face this issue.

Something that I wish this keyboard had is a touch pad. If this device can be both a keyboard and mouse, it would be much more useful.

Overall, the Samsers Wireless Portable Folding Keyboard is a good device but ultimately, it has a couple of shortcomings that keep it from being great.

title: Large 21" screen for better drawing experience
review_text:
I'm not a professional artist nor do I have a lot of experience with digital art, but that is one of the reasons that XP-Pen is a good choice for someone like me. Wacom rules the digital art world but for someone who is only a hobbyist when it comes to digital media, I have a hard time justifying paying the price that they charge. With that in mind, XP-Pen and Huion are the brands that I target for my budget.

Previously, I purchased a Huion Kamvas 13 and it was a great product but with my aging eyes, I needed a larger screen as even the 1080p resolution screen on that 13" screen was a little bit difficult for me to see without reading glasses. So when I had a chance to upgrade to a 21" XP-Pen, I took it.

This puts me in a situation where I am able to compare the two brands with each other. Both brands sport very similar pens and both screens have a matte surface to give the pens some friction for that "paper-like" feel. I'd say it's more like pen on paper feel, whereas I would've preferred to have more friction but it's something I think is worth training myself to get used to.

The XP-Pen drivers are on-par with the Huion drivers. Once the drivers are installed, it will show a preview of the screen layout that you have set up in Windows and it's quite easy to select the correct screen area that the pen should direct its touch to. From there, the pen buttons can be customized to macros that fit your needs and of course you can set up a different macro for each app that you use.

There are no additional macro assignable buttons on the XP-Pen screen, but there are standard OSD menu buttons at the top of the monitor, just like any other monitor you may own.

I'm happy to report that the XP-Pen drivers run alongside the Huion drivers without conflict. I have a Huion macro pad to make up for the buttons that are missing on the XP-Pen monitor.

So not being a professional artist, I do still try to spend as much time as I can to learn digital drawing and painting. In addition, I have interest in video and photo editing, so this pen tablet is great for selecting subjects using the rotoscope tool in video editor or smart select tools in image editors. Then there's 3D modeling. The pressure sensitive pen is great for sculpting in Blender and other 3D modeling programs. This is also something I'm trying to learn as well.

Despite the multitude of uses that I described above, I also don't have the desk space to devote to this 21" beast. It means that I needed a way to safely stow it. I didn't expect that I would find a carrying case for a large monitor, but to my surprise, that's exactly what I found! This [[ASIN:B099ZSDQ6V KISLANE travel carrying case]] fits the XP-Pen perfectly. It is big enough for the monitor, including its adjustable height stand and has plenty of pockets for the power adapter, pen, usb cables and my Huion macro pad. I didn't think there would be a market for people who thought "hey, it'd be great if I could bring my 24-inch iMac on my trip!", but thanks for that! Now I have a case for my 21" pen tablet.

One thing to note: I ran into an issue with inconsistent pressure with the XP-Pen drivers where I would run the pen across the scree and the darkness or width of the line would be very jittery. It was only alleviated by turning off the setting called Microsoft Ink. After my computer upgraded to Windows 11, I haven't seen this issue. So if it happens to you, try turning of that setting.

title: Attach my camera HOW?
review_text:
The premise with the ENSGO TC7 8” Teleprompter and others like it is to find a lens adapter that fits your camera and then screw it into your camera... then let your camera hang, by those threads, from the teleprompter. What??

First, the product: included in the box of the ENSGO TC7 8” Teleprompter is a set of lens adapters for common lens sizes going from 49mm to 82mm. There's also a bracket for a phone mount along with a couple of foam pieces to use with the phone adapter. Lastly, a bluetooth remote control for use with teleprompter apps.

If one follows the included directions or even use the product images as a guide, this would be the setup: Pick the correct adapter size and screws it to the lens of the camera. The adapter then slips into a slot in the main body of the product and from there, the tripod is mounted to the teleprompter or the camera. In either of these mounting scenarios, the thread holding the camera to the adapter is expected to hold the entire weight of the camera or the weight of the teleprompter + tablet. Please do NOT do this.

I use two tripods for this setup. One for the teleprompter and the other for the camera itself. I have yet figured out a secure bracket that would allow the camera to mount to the teleprompter without putting pressure on the screw threads.
